maintopic: BARRIEFIELD CAMP-QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
BARRIEFIELD CAMP-QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege.
I wish to call attention to an article in the last issue of the 'Military Gazette' which charges me with having made statements involving the good name of a Kingstonian, and with bringing discredit and dishonour on the Department of Militia and Defence. These statements have reference to my criticism of the expenditure on the servants cottages at the Royal Military College, Kingston. The justification for that criticism of mine is found in the fact that the Minister of Public Works himself, after giving consideration to the matter, reduced the item that I criticised, by $20,000. This article in the ' Military Gazette also charges me with reflecting on the Commandant and the entire staff,_ as well as on every officer, non-commissioned officer and soldier that attended the Barriefield camp last year. That allegation on the part of the writer has reference to a statement as to the drunkenness and brawling which I witnessed at Barriefield camp one Sunday, last year. I wish simply to say, Sir, that my remarks with regard to the camp_ were preceded by some remarks of the Liberal member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), which remarks were concurred in, almost to their entire extent, by the Minister of Militia himself. By reference to the statement of the Minister of Militia, it will be found that the personnel of the militia was not what it should be, and that the canteen was a nuisance which the department was endeavouring to regulate. I believe that the Minister of Militia would receive the en-dorsation of the people of this country, if he made an effort to control the sale of liquor at military camps. Now, Sir, I did not say that the men at the Barriefield camp were vicious and drunken; I did say that those in charge of the canteen were charged with selling liquor, and I repeat that statement now. One of the men charged was tried and convicted and fined for selling liquor; and, as regards the other men charged, the charge was amended by consent to having liquor in their possession, instead of selling it. All of these people pleaded guilty, and all of them were fined. In fact, the only regimental corps that was not fined was the 47th Battalion, which did not have any canteen. I repeat that I did not state in this House, as the article says, that the men at the Barriefield camp were vicious and drunken. I could

not have made that statement in truth, because I am very well acquainted with many of the men who attend that camp, and I know that some of them come from the most respected families in and around that district, and are orderly and respectable themselves. I repeat that there was drunkenness and brawling at the Barrie-field camp on Sunday afternoon. I have made careful inquiry into the matter, and it is only fair for me to state that in my belief most of that drunkenness and brawling was on the part of civilians, and not on the part of the soldiers themselves. In fact, I was more careful to investigate, on account of this matter being called to my attention by some of the officers from my locality, and, although drinking no doubt did exist in the camp there, as probably it will exist in any camp, yet I think it is quite possible that had it not been for the civilians who visited that camp, the drinking of the soldiers themselves would not have been noticed. I wish, further, to say, that in no way did I in my remarks on that occasion attribute any wrong to the Commandant, Colonel Gordon, or to the officers^ under him. I believe, Sir, that the fault, if fault there is, lies at the head of the Militia Department. From all I have been able to learn, and I desire to say it here now, I believe that the District Officer Comamnding at Kingston is an officer who well deserves the high reputation he enjoys in the vicinity in which he is best known.
I believe he is a gentleman who will carry out any instructions that are given him, and if the Minister of Militia should issue an order abolishing the canteen, I am firmly convinced that, so far as the camp at Bar-riefield is concerned, and so long as Colonel Gordon is in command, the instructions of the Minister of Militia will be carried out to the letter.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: CURRIE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 172) to amend the Railway Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this Bill is intended to correct what is a manifest error in the Act in reference to train men. The clause of the Act that I propose to amend provides that when a train is being backed or pushed in front of the locomotive a man must be stationed on top of the car leading. This is quite right, but it goes farther and says that if an engine is being backed up a man must be placed on the tender behind the engine. Everybody knows that the engineer upon an engine can see just as well behind the tender as he can see in front of the engine. There is no place for a brakem'an on the rear end of the tender. This rule is one which was avoided until the last year or two when the enforcement of the law became more stringent and trainmen were brought to book for what they did not do. It would be as fair to ask these men to sit on the cow catcher as to sit on the rear of the tender. The intention of the amendment is to strike out the line which says that a mqn must sit on the tender when the locomotive is backing up. A number of accidents have occurred and the men in my riding who are interested have requested me to endeavour to have this grievance removed. I hope the Minister of Railways will see his way clear to make this change in the law and to incorporate the principle of my Bill in any one of the many railway bills which he has on the order paper, before the end of the session.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: CURRIE (Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 173) to amend the Manitoba Grain Act.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: MANITOBA GRAIN ACT.
speechtext: This Bill is intended to correct a grievance under which the vessel men suffer. Most of the grain from the Northwest is shipped by rail to the head of the lakes and then carried by steamer to the terminal elevators on the lakes or to the sea-board. The law at present provides for the inspection of this grain, and that the certificates should follow it to the sea-board, which is a very wise provision. It provides also that the grain shall be weighed into the terminal elevator on the great lakes by special weighmen, and there is no provision in the law which renders it compulsory that the grain shall be weighed into the vessel and out of the vessel again. The result of that has been great loss to the steamship interests on the great lakes last year. The following were the shortages charged against the different companies named:-

maintopic: RAILWAY SUBSIDIES ACT-CLERICAL ERROR.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: RAILWAY SUBSIDIES ACT-CLERICAL ERROR.
speechtext: This Bill is to correct a peculiar error in the statutes of 1908. At page 1409 of the Votes and Proceedings of July last, the House went into Committee of the Whole to consider resolutions respecting railway subsidies, and among the subsidies was one to the Vancouver, Westminster and Yukon Railway, to aid towards the construction and completion of a railway bridge across Burrard inlet, the amount of the aid being $200,000. That resolution went through the House in its various stages, but to the astonishment of everybody, myself included, when the statute was printed, it was an absolute blank, so far as the amount was concerned.

speechtext: A typographical error?

speechtext:
Another typographical

speechtext: They will occur.

maintopic: RAILWAY SUBSIDIES ACT-CLERICAL ERROR.

speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways recognizes the possibility of these typographical errors. May I venture to hope that he will express to his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, the possibility of such typographical errors occurring even in well-ordered departments of the government. And may I cite this as the first instance within recent years at least, when such a typographical error has made necessary the enactment of a special Act of parliament. Perhaps the Minister of Railways will not be indisposed to extend the provisions of his Bill to certain other typographical errors to which attention has been directed in recent times.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

That on further considering the provisions of the said 45 Vic., chap. 34-1, the Provincial Secretary is of opinion that the company is by law entitled to be paid a subsidy at the rate of $3,000 per mile. No legislative authority for payment of said $8,000 is necessary.
These are the orders of Messrs. Pugsley, Skinner and Whitehead:
That the said sum of $13,000 as paid on account of work done by the Central Railway Company, and said amount should be deducted from the subsidy to be payable to the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, that the company is, however, willing that in addition to the said sum of $13,000, there shall also be retained by the province the further sum of $1,000, which, as the distance from Chipman to Gibson is 45 miles, would make the subsidy actually available to this company $2,500 per mile. It is recommended that there be paid to the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company the said sum of $8,500, the same to be chargeable against the said subsidy of $3,000 per mile, the same to be paid on the understanding with the said company that the said sum of $13,000, said sum of $8,500 to be now paid and said amount of $1,000, or $22,500 in all, shall be deducted from the subsidy of $3,000 per mile, payable under the said Act, so that the total remaining subsidy to be paid to the company (including said $5,000) shall be at the rate of $2,500 per mile, and that provincial debentures for the said amount to be issued by the Receiver General in amounts of $500 each, bearing interest at a rate not exceeding 4 per cent per annum, such debentures to be signed by the Provincial Secretary and to be under the great seal of the province; that the said debentures be issued as provided for by section 6 of the said Act, that the same be sold and the proceeds thereof applied to the payment of the said sum of $8,500.
That is the way, Mr. Speaker, that the difference in the aggregate of the amount in the subsidy payable under the contract with the company and the subsidy provided by the Act is accounted for; $13,000 having been previously paid, $2,250 of that on the orders of the Minister -of Public Works and Mr. Skinner, and $8,500 more on the same orders upon which $2,250 had been

paid and another $1,000 that seems to have been lifted at the same time. In view of these records, I think that the statement made by the Minister of Public Works about there being no ground for saying that there was any illegal payment of subsidies will not carry very much weight. The records show indisputably that the company received on account of this fifteen mile section $57,000 although under the contract they were entitled to be paid only $37,500 on account of the fifteen mile section. The statement will be found on page 42 of this case. There was paid on account of the fifteen mile section and the branches $77,000, of which $20,000 was for the branches, leaving $57,000 of subsidy paid to this company for fifteen miles where $45,000 was the maximum that was payable to the company under the provisions of the Act. There is no question but that that amount of $70,000, including the $13,000 previously paid, has been paid in subsidies under the Act of 1882 in respect of the main line and exclusive of the branches on account of which $20,000 was paid under a later Act, notwithstanding that only fifteen miles of railway have been built, which would justify a subsidy of $45,000. So that there has been illegally paid in connection with that fifteen mile section $25,000 of subsidy. I have already indicated what became of $8,500 of this amount, that amount having been paid under these orders which were held by the Minister of Public Works and Mr. Whitehead, and which appear in the records here as having been lodged with the deputy receiver general, and having been a first charge on the subsidy as it should be earned under the contract. There is another interesting fact in connection with the payment of this $2,250 to Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Skinner. I will put on the record the references in the report so that there may be no misapprehension. There will be found on the record an assignment from Dr. de Bertram to Wm. Pugsley and C. N. Skinner for $7,500 on pages 92 and 93. Then there is an order from Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Skinner to the receiver general to pay $2,750 to the Bank of New Brunswick at page 97. Then, the Attorney General, the late Mr. Blair, writes to the Deputy Receiver General inclosing the order of Messrs. Pugsley and Skinner and directing him to write to the Bank of New Brunswick stating that that $2,750 will be a first charge on the subsidy, and will be paid out of the first moneys earned-at page 98. The Deputy Receiver General accordingly writes to the bank-page 99. Then there is ' an order from Messrs Pugsley and Skinner to the Receiver General directing him to pay David O'Connell $2,000, and Mr. Pugsley incloses order to Mr. Babbitt, deputy 182
receiver general, the same day and asks that a letter be sent to Mr. O'Connell similar to the one that was sent to the Bank of New Brunswick. Mr. O'Connell, I may say, is a money lender in the city of St. John; so that Messrs. Pugsley and Skinner do not seem to have lost very much time in hypothecating the assignment of the subsidies they obtained. Then there is a further order signed by Messrs Pugsley and Skinner to the Receiver General for $550, and a letter asking the Receiver General to send to Mr. Trueman a letter addressed to the bank similar to the one that was sent to O'Connell; that is dated the 4th of January, 1896, and is found at page 103. So that there were orders outstanding against the $7,500 assignment, amounting to $5,300. I have already referred to the order in council that was passed providing for the payment of a further sum of $8,500 on account of these orders; and it is very significant that the Deputy Receiver General should be instructed later on to make a payment of $5,630 out of the subsidy that was paid under the order in council of 1902 to David O'Connell, the money lender, who was Mr. Pugsley's creditor under the other assignment, and that he should receive a payment out of a further subsidy that was voted by the provincial legislature and out of a subsidy that was paid illegally. So that when the records and the evidence are examined, it will be found that there has been no warrant, to say the least, for the statement that the Minister of Public Works has addressed to the House on this subject this afternoon. The Minister of Public Works has also stated that the reference made in this report to the guarantee of bonds is unfounded and false; he spoke of it as one of the most serious misrepresentations made in the report. The reference is to be found at page 19, beginning at the bottom of page 18:
Notwithstanding this fact, it appears conclusive from the evidence that the whole $250,000 par value of these 3 per cent bonds had been guaranteed and delivered to the company up to the 6th of August, 1903.
The evidence bears out that statement, but before proceeding to discuss that point and in order that the House may have a clearer understanding of this question of the guarantee of bonds, let me further refer to the legislation passed in that connection. In the session of 1901 an Act was passed incorporating the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company. During the same session another Act was passed authorizing the Lieutenant Governor in Council to guarantee the bonds of any company which would undertake to construct a line of railway from Cliipman to Gibson to the extent of $250,000 upon the conditions, however, set out clearly in", u"

the statute, that the province should not be liable for one cent or that any portion of the bonds should be guaranteed until the line was completely constructed and in operation and a certificate to that effect given by the government engineer. That Act was subject further to this distinct provision that the bonds should not be guaranteed until this company had established and in working order a mining plant capable of mining 500 tons of coal per day. Those were the conditions precedent to the right of the government to guarantee any bonds under the Act of 1901. There was, an Act passed in 1902 by the legislaturei amending that Act to this extent. Section one provides that notwithstanding the provisions of the Act of 1901 the Governor in Council may guarantee bonds upon progress estimates subject, however, to their not exceeding in amount the cost of the' work already completed relatively to the whole cost of the road, and also providing' that there shall be retained such an amount of first mortgage bonds, until the establishment of the mining plant provided for by such Act, as will, in the opinion of the* Lieutenant Governor in Council be sufficient to provide the cost thereof. That provision has never been removed or modified in any way with reference to the re-' taining of the bonds providing for a mining plant. This amendment I have quoted, although it provided for the issue of bonds upon progress estimates, provided also that there should be kept in mind the cost of1 the work already completed relatively to the whole cost of the road.
In the session of 1903 there was a further Act providing that there might be a further issue amounting to $200,000 for tha purchase of the Central Railway, the Act' setting out that $180,000 was to provide for the purchase price of the Railway and $20,000 to recoup the company for expensed made for the betterment of the road. In, 1904, a further Act was passed and that Act is rather an interesting one. It contains the section which the commission has spoken of as an obscure section, and which opinion the Minister of Public Works tried to make light of this afternoon. When hon. members see the manner in which this was smuggled into the Act they will conclude that the commission were quite justified in speaking of this provision in the way they did. The Act in question is entitled an Act to amend the law authorizing the granting of aid to certain railways. There are five sections in it. The New Brunswick Coal Company and Railway Company is mentioned in the recital and the first section confirms the purchase of the Central Railway by that Company. The second section relates to a distinct and separate railway, the Restigouche and Western Railway, and refers to an Act af-Mr. CROCKET.
fecting entirely that railway. Then the fourth reads:
If by reason of work on any section of the said line of railways being or having been found to be more than ordinarily expensive, it is found necessary to do so, the Provincial Secretary, by and with the authority of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, may endorse such guarantee on the bonds required to complete such road, and the amount of such guarantee may be greater than the mileage completed bears to the whole mileage of the line.
That section related to the Restigouche and Western Railway, and when the references made in that statute are looked up,i it will be seen that they deal entirely with that road. But what does the ingenious Attorney General of that province do in the same Act? He adds this as section 5:
Section 5. The said Act, Edward VII., chapter 41, shall be construed as if the provisions of section 4 had been enacted at the same time as said Act and as part thereof.
What member of this House is there who,
reading the provisions of that Act would have taken them to amend the Railway Act governing the guaraantee of bonds to the Central Railway. The provision for the guarantee of bonds regardless of mileage in section four related entirely to the Restigouche and Western. I ask if the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) who was then Attorney General of New Brunswick had wished the legislature to clearly understand the effect of the Act he was attempting to pass, he would have made a provision in the waj{\xa3it appears in this statute I have quoted. Why, when that Bill was brought down, the Hon. Mr. Hill, who was a strong supporter of the government, stated that he could not support the Bill because it referred to two different railways and was so mixed up that he could not understand its effect.
That was the way in which provision was made for the guaranteeing of bonds beyond the progress estimates proportioned upon the completed work in comparison with the whole mileage of the road. Now, bearing in mind this legislation, and bearing in mind the Act of 1901, I say, and the statement cannot be controverted, that there never was an amendment made to the Act of 1901 which did away with the provision requiring bonds to be retained for the purchase of a coal plant capable of mining 500 tons of coal per day, and which plant was estimated to cost $50,000. Furthermore, when we consider the Act of 1902, although it provided for the issue of bonds upon progress estimates, it was subject to the provision I have pointed out, that there must always be borne in mind the cost of the completed work relatively to the cost of the whole line, so that, until the Act of 1904, this section of 15 miles was

not entitled to any more than its proportion of the $250,000. The fact is that, notwithstanding that, before the Act of 1904 was passed, just as the commission has stated in its report, every dollar of the $250,000 bonds were guaranteed. The Minister of Public Works cannot dispute that statement. And not only that, but a further amount of $200,000, which was provided in the year 1903 for the purchase of the Central Railway, also had been exhausted, with the exception of $52,000, before the Act of 1904 was passed. Now, I ask any lawyer in this House, or any member of this House who cares to examine these statutes and orders in council, if it is possible for any one to claim that under that legislation, speaking of the issue and guarantee of bonds before the Act of 1904, the whole issue	could	legally have
been guaranteed.	There is absolutely
no question whatever that these bonds were guaranteed in contravention of the provision of he law,	and, in that
connection, it should be borne in mind that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) was responsible not only as ex officio director of the Coal Company for the distribution of moneys that went into the treasury of that company, but he was responsible as Attorney General and as a member of the Executive Council for the payment to that company of all moneys from the treasury of the province of New Brunswick. He not only disregarded all these provisions that had been mentioned, but did so in absolute violation of the law and without excuse or justification of any kind.
Proportioning the guarantee of bonds of $250,000 for the whole line of Tailway, 45 miles from Gibson to Chipman, the 15-mile section would have been entitled, of course, to one-third of that amount. But the Minister of Public Works, as Attorney General of the province, claimed that the first 15-mile section was costing more per mile than the unconstructed 30-mile section would cost, and that for that reason the 15-mile section was entitled to get more than one-third of the bonds. Now, if the evidence is turned up, it will be found, and found in the very document the Minister of Public Works read, bearing the signature of Mr. Evans, and dated 2nd January, 1903, that the estimated cost of the 15-mile section was $130,434, and of the 30-mile section $213,848, making a total of $344,282. That would leave less than 39 per cent for the 15-mile section and more than 61 per cent for the unconstructed 30-mile section. In addition, the Act provided that $50,000 should be retained for the mining plant. Deducting that, you find that $200,000 would remain and that the 39 per cent for the 15-mile section would amount to $78,000 and the 61 per cent for the 15-mile section would 182)
amount to $122,000. Besides this, the government had passed an order in council guaranteeing to the federal government the payment of $40,000 for rails advanced by the Intercolonial Railway for use on the 15-mile section and providing that the company should deposit their bonds with the Receiver General to cover the purchase price. This would leave but $38,000 as the maximum amount that could before the passing of the Act of 1904 have been legally guaranteed. Notwithstanding that, the Minister of Public Works was compelled to admit this evening that on August 6, 1903, $338,000 of bonds had been issued and guaranteed. It is true that he said $200,000 would be bonds authorized for the purchase of the Central Railway. But taking him even at that, there would be left $138,000 of bonds that had been issued before the passing of the Act of 1904 for the 15-mile section when, under the statute and orders in council, that section was entitled to receive but $38,000. So that, on his own statement, we find that the government of which the hon. gentleman was a member- and there is no doubt that he was responsible for all these transactions-issued bonds to the amount of $100,000 in absolute violation of the law.	_
There -are some other matters to which I wish to refer, and, as the hour is late, I will ask your permission, Mr. Speaker, to move the adjournment of the debate."]

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to direct attention to a matter compromising and reflecting upon the dignity of parliament and the dignity of the whole country as well, a matter in which, therefore every member of this House and every good citizen of this country must feel a keen interest and because of which he must feel deep humiliation. Every one regrets the necessity of introducing anything unpleasant into the deliberations of this House, and the task of doing so which I have undertaken is to me by no means a pleasant or agreeable one. Indeed, I realize it as both ungracious and unpleasant. For my part, there is, however, in this matter no animus whatever, it is purely a strong sense of public duty which impels me to move in the matter, a duty which every member of this House ought to feel when the interests of the country are involved, a duty which may not be ignored without incurring the justly merited condemnation of public opinion. I take it to be the clear duty of this House to maintain at all times a zealous guard over its honour and standing. Eepresenta-tives are sent to this House by their constituents to sift and inquire into public matters of every kind, to investigate everything of a public nature concerning the welfare of the country. The public acts of public men are public property, and the people have a right to know and, if need be, to inquire into these acts and ascertain of what character they are. The public conduct, past or present, of every officer of this House, of the Prime Minister of this country or any of his colleagues, of every member of this House, of every servant of this government adds to or subtracts from the aggregate public morality and dignity of this country. Any act in violation of strict rectitude on the part of public men, any want of zealous attention to the interest of the country, permeates the whole moral fabric of the people and causes its deterioration. And hence I have no apology to make for introducing the matters whch I am about to introduce.. I regard it as a duty, and I have no doubt every member of this House will take that view of it after he hears all that is to be said on the question.
Perhaps you will permit me, before going into the details of this matter, to call the attention of the House for one moment to the tender regard in which the reputation 1784
ot public men in England is held, not only by public men themselves, but by the whole people of the country. It is the practice in England, universally observed, _ that where a member of the government is reflected upon by the bench he does not wait to be asked to resign, he at once tenders his resignation. So careful are they in England to guard the reputations of their leading men, feeling and realizing that any other course, any imputation of improper conduct must be injurious to the whole moral fabric of the people. There are many cases that may be referred to, amongst others the Lord Lennox case, the Mundella case, the Mr. Stansfield case, and the Mr. Hayes Fisher case. When there was some question as to the conduct of Mr. Hayes Fisher as a member of a syndicate in consequence of remarks made by a judge upon the bench, Mr. Hayes Fisher used this language in the imperial House of Commons-Judge Buckley from the bench had said that Mr. Fisher and Sir Josepth Lawrence had left the entire management of the syndicate

Now, there was a court, Mr. Speaker, constituted as the ordinary courts of the land are constituted. The ordinary courts of the land are constituted by the various legislatures of the provinces, the legislatures determine the procedure, they determine the number of judges who shall be appointed, and when we are considering the report of this tribunal we are considering the report of a court regularly, legally, and constitutionally appointed, possessing all the powers and all the privileges and all the dignity and all the solemnity that attach to the courts of this land. The Minister of Public Works was a man who enjoyed nearly all of the highest honours that could be heaped upon him by the citizens of his native province. He was Speaker of the Legislative Assembly from 1887 to 1889, when he became Solicitor-General, and so continued until 1892; he was appointed Attorney General in the year 1900, and continued to be Attorney General until the year 1907, when for a short time he was premier, and afterwards in the month of August of that year, he was appointed Minister of Public Works of the Dominion. The order in council appointing the members of this tribunal is as follows: _ The Hon. the Attorney General-reports for the information, of the committee of the Executive Council:- , . , . Landry, one of the Puisne Judges of the Supreme Court of this province, Pulton MacDougali, of the city of Moncton, banker, and Almon I. And the committee of council concurring in the recommendation of the Hon. the Attorney General,
It is accordingly so ordered.

I submit that while that judgment stands, it is an imputation, a compromise and a reflection upon the dignity of this House and upon the dignity of the people of this country. That was clearly his duty. I am not here to say whether that judgment is right or wrong; but I am here to assume that it is right, and I submit that it was the clear duty of a minister of the Crown against whom a judgment of that kind has been pronounced, in the meantime to stand aside. I was pointing out the position that the hon. Minister of Public Works occupied when that court was constituted. He was a trustee from the year 1901 after this company was inaugurated to the year 1907, and his first duty was to see that the sections of the Act giving the government power to guarantee $250,000 of bonds were strictly carried out by the company, that the company kept books, that the books were audited semi-annually, that statements were filed with the provincial secretary every six months under oath, showing that the transactions, of the company were in the best interests'*of the people of the province of New Brunswick, or at least straightforward and honest. The hon. Minister of Public Works is not unfamiliar with large financial transactions. He is perfectly familiar with such transactions. He is not an ignorant man; he is a man of capacity, an astute lawyer, and a man who knew that both law and equity required that in the position he occupied he should keep strict account of the transactions of that company, and be in a position to render a strict and accurate and satisfactory accounting when it was called for. On the 3rd day of March, 1908, the government of the province of New Brunswick changed hands. Those who had been opposed to him in politics for some years came to

power. He knew that this court had been constituted by the local legislature afteT the new government came into power. He was subpoenaed, as I am informed and believe, and was asked to produce all the documents and papers that he had in his possession to assist this court in ferreting out the matters for which they were appointed. He appeared before that court. There was able and devoted counsel there, perhaps not appointed by him, but I understand appointed at his suggestion to assist him in cross-examining witnesses. We have become painfully convinced after examining tbe evidence and the documents submitted to us that in the expenditure ^ of the public funds, provided for this enterprise, every person charged with a public duty in connection with the same, has been culpably negligent in the discharge of such duty. The degree of culpability attached to each individual has, perhaps, not been the same. Some were guilty of negligence in accepting positions of trust and in not acquainting themselves with what was transpiring in regard to same, but allowing others, unquestioned, to undertake the sole discharge of duties, the responsibility of which they themselves had assumed. They lent their names and allowed the moral influence of their high standing in the community to assure the province that legitimate business methods would be followed. The provincial secretary and the attorney general, ex-officio directors, who were specially appointed by the legislature to watch the company's doings in the interest of the province, we consider, by their conduct, open to the gravest censure. It is true the provincial secretary was not satisfied with matters as they were going, for more than once we find, by letter or otherwise, he registered objections-but it would seem he had assisted to call into play forces he could not control, if he wished to do so, and the bonds were in due course guaranteed and the moneys spent under the conditions stated in this report.
To sum up, on the evidence given before this court, under the sanction of an oath- the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) having appeared before the commissioners and counsel being present to act for and against him-this report constitutes the following findings:
1.	That he was appointed a director exofficio of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company specially to guard the people's interest and that he was in effect general manager of its affairs.
2.	That, while he was occupying this position of trust, charged with the performance of a public duty, in the expenditure of public funds provided by the people of New Brunswick for a public enterprise, he was culpably negligent and open to the gravest censure.
3.	That, although he was the controlling influence in the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, it never performed the functions usually exercised by an incorporated company and was in fact nothing but a disorganized department of the government.
4.	That in order to conceal the truth he adopted no system of bookkeeping for public information.
5.	That as a member of the Legislative Assembly and Attorney General of the Province, he made incorrect statements to the legislature'to allay suspicions and to conceal from the province the true state of ariairs.

Every member in this House is interested in seeing to it that every other member gets absolute justice and absolute fair play. I shall endeavour to assist in securing for every member of this House, whether on this side or on the other side, absolute justice and absolute fair play, as I would desire to have myself.
As the position of the Hon. L. J. Tweedie, Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, differed materially from that of the hon. Minister of Public Works in the transactions referred to in the report re the Central Eailway, I have not introduced

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am sorry that matters relating to what may be called the provincial sphere of politics, with which I was connected some years ago, should engage so much of the attention of this House to-day, yet, for myself, Sir, I am glad that the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has brought the matter before the House, because this report to which he has referred has been published broadcast in the newspapers, and the fact of his bringing the matter before parliament to-Mr. CROTHERS.
day gives me an opportunity of directing the attention of the House and of the country to it. I think, Sir, that, before I take my seat, I will be able to show that not only is this report one which ought not to be acted upon by men who desire to do justice, but that it is a report which, within the pages of the report itself, is discredited, shown to be of a partisan character and wholly unreliable. When I tell you, and when I tell this House that these commissi oneps, while attempting to give a statement of the interest that was expended by this company from the commencement of this transaction in 1901 down to the time when the commissioners, who had been appointed by the previous government went out of office, on the 31st March, 1908, only included two items of interest, one the interest upon the cost of the new line of railway during its construction and limited to the month of January, 1904, and another item beginning upon the 1st July, 1905, and closing upon the 31st March, 1908; when I tell you that these are the only two items of interest which they allow and which amount in themselves to, in the vicinity of, $5,000 more than the total interest which they allow; when I tell you that they leave out of this account every dollar of interest upon the total expenditure between the 1st day of January, 1904, and the 1st day of July, 1905, a period of eighteen months, and when I tell you further that they absolutely leave out of their calculation every dollar of interest upon the $180,000 which was paid for the Central Railway, upon the $77,000 of improvements which were made upon the Central Railway, upon the loss in operating, extending over a number of years, and upon other amounts, and that they have absolutely omitted these from the account and statement of interest which they give, I think you will be prepared to accept the statement which I shall make that this report is utterly unworthy of the consideration of any man who desires to see justice shown to a public man.
Without going further and dealing with other matters, let me prove this, because if I cannot prove this I have made a statement which ought to discredit me among the members of this House. Turn now, and let the hon. member for Elgin turn, if he wants to be fair

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I think he ought to remain here to hear the statement which I am to make, because I am satisfied that it will convince even him that this report, so far from having been prepared by an honest and non-partisan commission, so far from being a judicial report, has been prepared by a partisan counsel who has advised these commissioners in regard to it and who was instrumental in having it drawn up. My hon. friend has said that

upon this report and without considering whether it is true or false, without considering whether or not there is evidence to support it and to justify these commissioners in making it, I, as Minister of Public Works, ought to resign my __ seat. He quotes a statement of Mr. Fisher in the British parliament that when a charge was made against him he felt it his duty to resign. But in that.case Mr. Fisher said: I accept the judgment of the tribunal, in which I have confidence, and therefore I resign my seat. But, Sir, am I to accept the judgment of a partisan tribunal, a tribunal appointed not to inquire into the truth, but a tribunal appointed to find out something upon which a charge might be made against me in order that the wishes of those gentlemen who instituted these proceedings might be carried out, and whose typographical errors, as has been called to my attention, are already a joke throughout this country. I am prepared to take my position anywhere in this House or anywhere 'before the people of Canada and meet any charges which can be imade against me, and I do think, Sir, that it would have been the more constitutional course, the more dignified and the fairer course for the hon. member for Elgin, who reads this report and seeks to discredit me in the eyes of the people, to have read the evidence and to have seen if there was anything in the evidence which justifies the report. Then, if he had read the evidence the manly course for him, if he believed in the truth of these charges, would have been to have made boldly and openly a charge against me on the floor of this House. But, the hon. gentleman does not do that. He simply reads a report made in another place, made in reference to matters which in no way relate to this parliament or to Dominion affairs. In that report there is no charge made against my personal honour, there is no charge made that one dollhr of the moneys of this company ever came improperly into my hands. But the hon. gentleman, upon that report, taking up its various paragraphs charging neglect of my duty as Attorney General of the province, asks this parliament to take action and invites me to resign my seat. Well, Sir, while I am prepared to fight my enemies, and I have some, I am not prepared to lie down and let them crawl over me For twenty-four years I have fought them before the people of my native province, and whenever I have appealed to the people in my province I have not appealed in vain I said that these commissioners had absolutely omitted the interest upon this whole amount of indebtedness for a period of a year and a half. I stated also that they had omitted the interest upon all the amounts which were paid for the Central Railwav and the amounts which were disbursed for the improvement and operation of that railway, and I am going to prove it to you. At page 22 of the repott,
referring to the cost of the 15 mile section between Chipman and the coal fields of Minto and the branches to the various coal mines it says:
There is included in the above item of cost $316,626.33, the cost of the rolling stock $26,800, and we have included in the item ol interest in statement (c) the amount ol interest which he '(referring to Mr. Shannon, accountant of the Department of Railways) fixed at $28,231.63.
That is, Mr. Shannon fixed the interest at that amount. Then on page 23 it says:

At page 23 the commissioners say:
and so far as the evidence shows they were paid they are included in statement (c). Mr. Pugsley also in his statement of cost adopts Mr. Shannon's statement of interest during construction, namely, $28,231.63.
That statement of interest was made by Mr. Shannon who was the accountant of the Department of Railways in connection with the contention which the railway company was making that the interest during construction of the new' line should be added to capital, should form a part of the cost of construction, and therefore should be considered by the Department of Railways upon the question of whether they should pay the increased subsidy or not. Now then, the commissioners say they adopt that statement of $28,234, as the interest upon the cost of construction of the new line and they say it for two reasons. They say that Mr. Sharpe the accountant who made the interest at $33,000 had made it too large, and they take Mr. Shannon's statement which would be to the time of the completion of the first of January, 1904. They adopt Mt. Shannon's interest for that
reason and they adopt it also

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I thought the language of the report was that the hon. gentleman himself adopted it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Yes. Their other reason which I was about to state is that they say they adopted it because Mr. Pugsley him-

self adopted it at the time. When I adopted it was when I was urging the favourable consideration of the company's claim before the Department of Railways, putting forward that Mr. Shannon himself had found that the interest upon the cost of construction amounted to $28,234 and I urged that there was no other account to which it could be charged, that interest during construction should be properly added to the cost, and that therefore this should be taken into consideration by the Department of Railways. _ Now, we start there with the amount admitted by the commissioners and found by Mr. Shannon to be the interest upqn the cost of construction of the 15 mile section and branches to the 1st of January, 1904, when the road was substantially completed, or at all events I think the main line was entirely completed. Then if you turn to pages 79 and 80 of this report you will find they give a statement of the moneys received and the moneys paid out in connection -with the railway and branches since taken over by the province on the 1st of July, 1905. Let me read this again so that there may be no misunderstanding :
Moneys received and moneys paid nut in connection with the railway and branches since taken over by province, July 1, 1905.
Interest on loans and coupons, $68,770.65
Now, if you add together the $28,234 which they say was the interest upon the cost of construction of the new line to the month of January, 1904, and the $68,770 which they say was expended in interest subsequent to the 1st of July, 1905, and you get nearly $97,000 of interest, and yet, Sir, upon page 76 of this report these commissioners in arriving at this shortage put in the total amount of interest over the whole period and upon all the expenditures of the company at $92,000, being $5,000 less than the two items alone of interest to which I have called your attention. Is that another typograohical error?
Then, if you turn back a little bit farther in the report you will find that in giving a statement with regard to some moneys which were due to the Peoples' Bank at Fredericton alone, you will find that they show there that up to the 1st of January there was a note due to the Peoples' Bank of New Brunswick amounting to $169,314.94, and that interest charges to October 14, 1905, brought the total up to $176,611.53, or interest of about $7,000 which was paid to the Peoples' Bank of New Brunswick subsequent to the 1st of January, 1904, and with the exception of the interest between the 1st of July and October they have left that out of the account altogether as well. And as I have said, there is the total interest upon the cost of the new line, $316,000. which they find to be correct, upon the $180,000 expended for the purchase Mr. PUGSLEY.
of the Central Railway, upon the improvements of $77,000 which were placed upon the Central Railway according to the report of these commissioners, and they leave all of the interest upon that large amount out for a period of 18 months during a portion of which period as the commissioners themselves say the company was paying interest at a rate of from 6j per cent to 7 per cent. And in addition to that they leave out, prior to the 1st of January, 1904, all the interest upon the cost of the Central Railway and upon the improvements which were made to the Central.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I shall show a little later that in the desire of these commissioners to submit a report upon which some action might be taken adverse to myself, they either wittingly or unwittingly omitted to include interest which I venture to say would amount to somewhere in the vicinity of $60,000. And I would invite my hon. friend the member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) to explain how it is that he can justify the report of the commissioners who, in an attempt to arrive at the expenditure on this road utterly and absolutely ignore the interest extending over these lengthy periods and upon these large amounts of money, which would necessarily come to a very large sum?
Now, Sir, there is no excuse for these commissioners. They were not bound to take Mr. Shannon's statement of the interest on the cost of construction of the new line down to January 1, 1904, they were not bound to take my statement either, because under the authority which -the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crothers) has read the statute clothed them with power to summon before them every person who they thought might give evidence which would be of importance to the commission. They were empowered to bring any acounts before them and they could have subpoenaed the managers of the various banks. They were notified that the loans for this company had been negotiated at the Peoples' Bank of New Brunswick, at the Bank of Montreal, Fredericton, through Mr. G. W. Allen, the secretary of the company, at the Bank of British North America in Fredericton, through Mr. Allen, the secretary of the company; that an account had at my request been opened for the company with the Bank of New Brunswick in the city of St. John, and they had before them also the fact that loans were negotiated with the Canada Permanent Mortgage Company and that there were loans also from the Bank of Nova Scotia in St. John. They had before them the names of all these banks and of the loan company from whom the company had received loans from time to time. As every hon. member in this House knows, when a note is taken to a bank for discount the proceeds of the note

less the discount are paid to the credit of the person or company that obtains the discount. And in every case the accounts of these banks would show what was the discount taken off these notes from time to time and paid by the company. Therefore, these commissioners had it in their power to obtain from the managers and accountants of these various banks the interest which was paid by this company during that long period of seven years, extending from 1901 to 1908. But, Sir, 1 am told by my hon. friend who represents the county of Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell), and who was present at this investigation as council, that, so far as the evidence showed, never once did they inquire of those institutions what was the interest paid by the company from time to time during this long period of years; and from the beginning to the end they never hinted that they wanted any information from the company with regard to the interest, and they left me, and I presume my hon. friend to assume that they would, before they came to the close of their investigation, have an accountant go through the books of the banks, ascertain what the interest was, and make a correct statement with regard to it; because, without a correct statement with regard to the interest, 1 ask what is the value of this report? In making the statement that there is a great deficiency between the receipts and the expenditures, they simply convey false information to the people of this country. Surely, Sir, it was the very least of the duties which they owed to the public and to those whose reputation was 'to a certain extent involved in the investigation, to make an inquiry into the interest, instead of simply adding those two sums together, one on a certain portion of the cost down to January, 1904, and the other on the cost down from the 1st of July, 1905, lumping tho_se two together, and arbitrarily throwing off $5,000 and fixing that as being approximately the interest which the company paid during that long period of years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I understand that the hon. gentleman had counsel there. If he had, why did not his counsel produce this evidence which he is bemoaning the loss of?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I have already stated why. The commissioners subpoenaed the banks with the accounts. They had brought to the city of St. John, some two or three weeks before the general election, an accountant for the purpose of going into these matters, and we had a right to assume that they would endeavour to give an accurate account, and would not arbitrarily fix the interest at some $60,000 less than the interest amounted to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: But when the evidence was not given

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I will ask the hon. gentleman's permission to ask him a question. I do not think the other hon. gentlemen opposite are acting very properly. If the Minister of Public Works does not want me to ask the question, I will not do so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I will be very glad to have the hon. gentleman ask it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Then I ask that hon. gentlemen do not interrupt in that very rude way. I wish to ask: Was there not a time in the investigation when the loss of this evidence was noticed? If so, why was not the evidence produced by the counsel appearing for the hon. gentleman?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
It was never intimated that there was any loss ot this evidence. The commissioners never intimated to my hon. friend from Carleton or to me, but that they were having the interest accurately made up, and it came to me as a shocking surprise when I read this report and found that they had simply taken the interest during the cost of construction of the new line to January, 1904, and the interest for the last 18 months or so and added those together, ignoring some $50,000 or $60,000 of interest, the particulars of which we had a right to suppose they were obtaining from the banks. When I tell this House that there would be interest on the cost of the Central Railway amounting to $180,000, interest on the improvements amounting to $77,000 and upwards, interest on loss of operation amounting to some $19,000, interest on the cost of some of the rolling stock, which was not added to the cost of construction, and interest on other expenditures in connection with the preliminary work which the company did with a view to carrying on mining operations, and when, as the commissioners themselves say, in many cases interest at the rate of 6i or 7 per cent was necessarily paid to the banks, they will see to what a large amount the interest would necessarily run up, and how necessary it was for these commissioners, if they wanted to give an accurate statement of the receipts and disbursements, to have a proper interest account made up. That they did not is itself evidence of the grossest possible _ carelessness on the part of these commissioners. It is more than that: It is evidence of a reckless desire to injure me and other members of the government in which I occupied the position of Attorney General. It is evidence that they thought that if they could get launched a report sufficiently strong, they might accomplish the

mission for which they were appointed- bring about my resignation, and leave me afterwards to vindicate' myself as best I could before the people of this country. It is evidence that these. commissioners did not care whether they did justice or a gross injustice, because in order to do justice it was absolutely essential that the report should be accurate, and should show with as much certainty as possible what were the receipts, and expenditures of this company.
That these commissioners and those advising them were actuated by partisan motives, I will show by another fact. It is this, that the public reports of the province of New Brunswick, the report of the Auditor General for the year 1908, show that in the month of October last, just before the general election, these commissioners employed Mr. Dunlop, a chartered accountant of, as I understand, the city of Montreal, and brought him down to St. John for the purpose of going into these accounts, and he made up a statement for them. That statement was published by Mr. H. A. Powell, the solicitor and counsel for these commissioners, and for the government of New Brunswick, and it appeared in the 'Daily Standard,' the Conservative organ of the city of St. John, in its issue of the 14th of October, 1908. What do you think, Sir, of commissioners who were engaged, as the hon. member for West Elgin says, upon a judicial inquiry, and who had not yet terminated their inquiry, upon the eve of an election in which I was a candidate, sending to the city of Montreal for an accountant and bringing him down to the city of St. John at the expense of the provincial government to have him investigate these accounts, and having published through Mr. Powell, the counsel for these commissioners, a statement of the professed receipts and disbursements doing that, as I say, before the commissioners had ended their labours and made their report, and doing it for no other purpose than to influence the people of New Brunswick against me? That statement, Sir, is worse than the statement which these commissioners have presented because it showed a deficiency of $117,000, and in addition Mr. Powell was reported in the newspaper as saying that Mr. Evans stated that there was a shortage in his payment of $47,000 ; and they put it before the people of St. John and the people of New Brunswick that there was a deficiency of $164,000 in connection with the Central Railway and the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, and because of this alleged deficiency they asked the people of New Brunswick to condemn me and my colleagues. I say that this is evidence of partisanship of the grossest character. I want to know what Mr. PUGSLEY.
the commissioners had to do with the general elections of the 26th of October, and what business it was of theirs to employ an accountant for the purpose of spreading that statement broadcast before the people of New Brunswick pending the completion of their report. But they had that prepared and published on the 14th of October, some 12 days before the general election. Fortunately I was able to show, by facts of the most convincing character, that the statement published in the 'Daily Standard ' alleged to have been made by Mr. Dunlop, was absolutely erroneous. I showed that certain facts and information must have been withheld from him which, if they had been furnished, would have compelled him to present a different report; and after I had made my statement and the errors in his report were shown, we heard little or nothing more of that report during the last few days preceding the general election.

speechtext: Having had this notice on the 14th of October, and not being examined before the end of December, why did the hon. gentleman not produce all this evidence which he said was available?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend why. This evidence was all available for the commissioners if they had chosen to ask for it; but from what I saw from the course of events in the newspapers-and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) will corroborate what I say-these commissioners, perhaps because they were guided by their counsel, did not act as if they wanted it. They did not go along in a connected way to get the receipts and disbursements, but they got a little evidence

here and a little there, they called first one man and then another, and presented the evidence in a disconnected way, so that no one could follow it or suspect what these commissioners were going to do when they finally decided to make up their report. They did not do what they ought to have done, if they expected to treat this company as trustees and were going to have a report or an accounting from them. If they had wanted to do that, what was the proper course open to them? Their proper course was to notify the president of the company that they were commissioners appointed by the provincial legislature to inquire into this matter, and ask this company to file an account from beginning to end, showing its receipts and disbursements. That is what is done every day in a court of equity.

And yet, Sir, there appears upon this report the damning insinuation that Hon. F. P. Thompson had received as graft the proceeds of this note of $10,000. Now, does not this impress this House, and even gentlemen upon the other side, particularly the legal members, that if these commissioners and their counsel had been actuated by any sense of fair play, when they came across the entry of this note in the bank marked with the initials ' F.P.T.' they would have sent for Mr. Thompson and asked an explanation? It would have been a simple thing to say:	We
find your initials on this note, we cannot trace the proceeds, and would like you to give us information concerning it. Would not that have been the fair, the honest, the decent thing to do?-to say nothing more. Now, I will give you another evidence of the unfairness of these commissioners. By the statement which the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has read, and by the order in council appointing these commissioners, they were limited in their duties to an examination into the expenditures which were made subsequent to January 1, 1901, in connection with this railway. Let me read it. You will find it at page 8 of the report:
By the terms of the statute authorizing the investigation, we were authorized and directed to inquire into and report upon the following matters:	,
1.	The expenditures of all provincial moneys from the 1st of January, 1901, in connection "dth the road from Norton to Gibson and all branches.
Well, Sir, when these commissioners went through matters-as I suppose-as they came to their notice, apparently they were not able to find that there had been any money that had come improperly into my hands or into the hands of the other directors of the company, because the evidence shows that the proceeds of any notes with the discounting of which I had nothing to do were handed over to the contractors and the secretary of the company whose duty it was to keep the accounts. Not finding anything to impeach my honour, or to show that I have received any part of this money, they thought that they would extend their duties a little further. Though the Act limited them to 1901, they thought they would go back. They thought they might find something against the government in 1890, when Mr. Blair was leader of the government, and. in order to gratify their hatred of an Mr. PUGSLEY.
old political opponent, they went back- how far do you think, Mr. Speaker? They went back to 1887, fourteen years before the time named in the statute and in the order in council appointing them. And they say that, in connection with certain matters regarding the subsidies, he was generously paid but the amount of which they had been unable to determine. And again they make a statement with regard to Mr. Blair in which they charge that there was a holdup or graft of which Mr. Blair, as leader of the government, was guilty, a statement which, I am informed by those who were interested in the company at that time, is absolutely untrue, a statement for which there is not a shadow of foundation. And yet these commissioners, in order to attack the memory of a man who never was afraid to stand up before them when he was living, and who has now passed over to the majority, go out of their way to make these charges of what took place fourteen years before the time concerning which their investigation was supposed to be held. They are not content to go back and attack the character of Mr. Blair, but they think they will get something against me by stating, as they do on page 4:
On October 4, 1895, a contract was entered mto by the New Brunswick government with the Central Railway Company for the construction of the fifteen mile section and the granting of the subsidy of $3,000 per mile. The following day $7,000 of this subsidy was assigned by Dr. de Bertram to the Hon William Pugsley and Mr. Skinner.
They say afterwards that upon that order $2,200 was paid. Well, Sir, I would ask any hon. member of this House if the commissioners might not reasonably expect that the inference to be drawn from that statement would be that this order in council, this order upon the subsidy, had been assigned to me while I was a member of the government, and that I received this $2,200 while I was a member of the government? They speak of me as the Honourable William Pugsley and say that it was to me that order was given, that it was to me it was paid jointly with Mr. Skinner. I-t may be said: 'They do not say that you were a member of the government at the time.' But they do not take any pains to inform the country that I was not a member of the government at the time. It happened that I had been a member of the government between 1890 and 1892, but in the latter year I went out of politics and remained out of politics for seven years; and, at the time when this transaction took place, I was not a member of the government nor even a member of the legislature, but I was solicitor for one of the parties interested in that contract and in the undertaking and had something to do with the transactions between Dr. de Bertram and the

James Barnes Company, -but my relations with them were wholly those of solicitor and client. Yet, notwithstanding that, the impression is sought to be created by this report that I was at that time a member of this government.

I am not stating what it was for. I think that what I have stated is enough for this House, though it may not
be for those who would make insinuations or imputations against me. I know there are a great many small men in the province of New Brunswick, narrow-minded men who, though having no evidence or facts to go upon, are always willing to make insinuations against their neighbours, and particularly against those who have been a little more successful in life than they themselves have been. It is enough for me to say that I was in some way, I do not remember, just how, for it was a long time, 14 years ago, acting in that case, either for Dr. de Bertram or James Barnes, the contractor, but I was not in politics, I was not a member of the government and not even a member of the legislature, and yet these commissioners went back in this case six years before the time which was named by the commission in order to throw out something as against myself which might be taken hold of by people who were not thoroughly informed with regard to the facts.
The commissioners go on to say also that there was something wrong with regard to a payment of $5,000 made to Dr. de Bertram when Mr. Blair was leader of the government. What that has to do with the matter I am unable to say, but since they mention it I will say that I made inquiry with regard to that and the circumstances were these:	The provincial government, away back in 1889 or 1890, at a time when Mr. Blair was the leader, had entered into a contract with the Central Railway Company of which Dr. de Bertram was .the assignee and contractor, for the construction of the line between Chip-man and Fredericton. Shortly after he had commenced work, this House, at the instance of the government of Sir John A. Macdonald, passed an Act for the construction of a railway between Harvey and Salisbury, what is known as the Harvey-Salisbury line, and that railway, for a considerable part of its course, would traverse the same route as was provided for in the contract between the government of New Brunswick and the Central Railway Company. Mr. Blair was of the opinion that if the Dominion government was going to subsidize the line it should not be built at the expense of the provincial government
and that no subsidy should be given by the New Brunswick legislature. He introduced an act in the legislature or had an order in council passed, authorizing him to stop the Work which Dr. de Bertram was doing and had a right to do under the terms of his contract. Although Dr. de Bertram had done work to the extent of some $13,000, if I remember the figures correctly, or perhaps a little less, he was stopped and the work was not proceeded with for the reason I have mentioned. The government of New Brunswick then led by Mr. Blair, paid to Dr. de Bertram as compensation for this work, which amounted to some $9,000 or $10,000, or $13,000, the sum of $5,000, and that was all that Dr. de Bertram got out of the transaction at the time, even although he had a perfect right to go on with his contract, -and although it seemed to me that the provincial government might well have paid him a larger sum under the circumstances in view of their having prevented him from having completed the work for which the government had agreed to pay him a subsidy. The commissioners speak further with reference to that and say there was some $8,000 which was paid illegally by the old government. As they have referred to it of course it is my duty to speak of it, because I notice that the commissioners say, and this was dwelt upon by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Croth-ers), that the $25,000 of subsidy which was paid under the old agreement and upon the work between Minto and Fredericton, or if you like between Chipman and Fredericton, it makes but little difference which so far as the argument is concerned, was illegally paid. The ground on which they based that assertion is that the subsidy was not to be paid except as each ten miles was completed. These commissioners do not deny that the work was done, they admit that Dr. de Bertram did between $33,000 and $36,000 worth of work, but they say that he had not finished up his ten mile section and that therefore the government of Mr. Blair acted illegally in making a payment of subsidy to him. These commissioners have forgotten that although under the terms of the contract the government was not bound to pay until and unless each section of ten miles was completed, yet, under the terms of the statute by virtue of which the subsidy was payable, the government was authorized to make a payment of 40 per cent as $20,000 worth of work was done from time to time. In other words they could pay on progress estimates 40 per cent of the work actually done and if this work wa3 done to the extent of $33,000 or $36,000, 40 per cent of that would amount to some $13,000, which would quite justify the government of Mr. Blair in paying the total

amount of subsidy to Dr. de Bertram as they did. Yet it is strongly put forward in this report that the whole issue was illegal and therefore I suppose that is part of the indictment which my hon. friend says he has presented against me because I was at one time a member of the government of Mr. Blair. Now we will see if we cannot find a fourth misstatement in the report.

They were not guaranteed bonds, they were not what is referred to by the reference at all. The reference was distinctly confined to the year 1901, by the statute.
I wish to invite attention to another statement which I think is of great importance, and which no member of this House should have been prepared to practically support by bringing this matter before the House unless he had made some inquiry and satisfied himself of its truthfulness. I find, on pages 18 and 19 of the report of the commissioners, a very important statement, and I am going to press this with a great deal of force, if I can press any point with force. I am going to urge upon the consideration of this House, the fact that not only is the statement to which I am about to allude false, but that it is, I am obliged to say, either knowingly or recklessly false. It has been made either knowing that it was false or with an utter disregard of the facts of the case. On page 18 they say:
Notwithstanding this fact, it appears conclusively from the evidence that the whole $250,000 par value of these 3 per cent bonds had been guaranteed and delivered to the company up to the 6th day of August, 1903.
That is a charge of the most serious character to make against the provincial government. That is a charge that we, in violation of the statute, in violation of our duty, when we had no legislative authority to do it, prior to the passing of the Act of 1904, which extended the powers as far as the guaranteeing of bonds was concerned, prior to the 6th of August, 1903, guaranteed the whole of this issue of $250,000 of three per cent bonds and that they were delivered to the company. They say that that appears conclusively from the evidence. I say it does not appear, not merely conclusively from the evidence, but that it does not appear at all from the evidence and that the evidence is entirely contrary to that, statement. So far from the whole $250,000 having been guaranteed prior to the 6th of August, 1903, the total amount which was guaranteed was $138,500, a difference of $111,500, between what was actually guaranteed and the statement which these commissioners make as the amount having been guaranteed. There is no excuse for that and it cannot be a typographical error either.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: It is a typical error.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Yes, it is a typical error though not a typographical one. On the 6th August, when the completion of the purchase of this Central Railway was about being effected and in respect to the Central Railway, the government was, by an Act of the legislature, authorized to guarantee bonds to the extent of $200,000.

Shadbolt, the manager of the Bank of Montreal and of the Royal Trust Company at St. John, in his evidence, produced a copy of this order before the commissioners, and it appears in the evidence upon which they ought to have made their report. If they had based their report upon the evidence, they would have known, they must have known that the total issue at that date included the $200,000 authorized to be guaranteed for the purchase of and improvements upon the Central Railway making a total of $338,500 or $111,500 more than these commissioners state had been issued.
