speechtext: And that the conveyance was not made until the date that the minister has referred to?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. The conveyance was made at that time simultaneously with it, and I may say to my hon. friend that as a portion of the conveyance and showing the care which I, as attorney general, exercised in connection with it, I insisted that some $66,000 of the bonds should be used in the Bank of New Brunswick and that all the outstanding mortgage bonds upon the road, amounting to $540,000, should be transferred to the vaults of the Bank of New Brunswick and kept there for the protection of the government and of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company until we had the whole title completed and everything carried out in accordance with the provisions of the Act of the legislature. The provisions of the statute were carried out to the letter and the complete title was vested in the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company. Under these circumstances, when the hon. member for Elgin talks, and when these commissioners talk about our having deceived the legislature, if they will look at the synoptic report of the proceedings of the legislature for the year 1904 they will find a full, a complete and a true statement in regard to the issue of the bonds. I have here a copy of the synoptic reports from the year 1901 to the year 1907 which I will be glad to submit to any hon. member of this House. They contain a statement of the total cost of the Tailway, of which I am going to speak in a little while, and of the issue of bonds, and so far as the cost of the construction of this railway is concerned, so far as the receipts and disbursements are concerned, so far as the issue of bonds which were made from time to time are concerned, so far as the various orders in council which were passed from time to time are concerned, I challenge any hon. member to take these reports from 1901 to 1907, during the time when these matters were being discussed, and point out where a single erroneous statement in regard to the cost or the issue of bonds was made to the legislature or that we in any way deceived them. It is all very well for these commissioners to say, as they do say, in a part of their report, that the fact of our being ex-officio members of this company gave us the opportunity to present such statements as were necessary to allay the suspicion of the legislature and to conceal from the country the true state of affairs. Surely it was the duty of these commissioners, before making a charge of such a serious character against public men, and before send-

ing that report broadcast throughout the country without the evidence, because the evidence has not been printed to this day, the provincial government, when requested to do so by the opposition in the New Brunswick legislature having refused to print it, to have shown, that we had presented false statements to the legislature, that we had concealed from the legislature the number and amount of the bonds which we had guaranteed from time to time and that we had made false statements as to the cost of the construction of this line, seeing that they were a judicial, and an impartial body prepared to do justice. Do you not think that the hon. member for Elgin, in carrying out the strong desire which he expressed to do justice even to the Minister of Public Works, notwithstanding his recent visit to St. John and consultation with those who were seeking to post him in regard to this inquiry, and before he would have placed upon the records of this House the statement that the attorney general and provincial secretary, by reason of their being ex-officio members of this company, were able, from their knowledge and control of the company's affairs to present such statements as were necessary to allay the suspicions of the legislature and conceal from the country the true state of affairs, would have felt it to be his duty to have shown that we had concealed from the legislature the number and amount of bonds which had been guaranteed from time to time and that we had concealed the amount which this road was costing.
Why, Sir, if you will turn to the debates of the legislature you will find that this matter came up for discussion session after session for a number of years and that every information was given in relation to it. It was a fruitful theme for discussion, the people were interested; the road was costing more than we had anticipated, the Central Railway upon which considerable improvements had been made and which was the key of the situation as connecting the Intercolonial with these large, valuable coal fields, had been unfortunate because of an accident that happened to one of the bridges; large expenses had to be incurred and there was a great deal of disappointment. The people were taking a great interest in the matter and it was discussed from time to time in the legislature, and we were asked from session to session: What is the amount of bonds that have been issued, what is the cost of the road, to what different people is the company indebted, what is the output of the mines, what is, the traffic upon the road, what are the receipts and the operating expenses? And, session after session in the minutest detail all that information was given to the House and to the people. I defy any hon. gentle-Mr. PUGSLEY.
man in this House to take the synoptic report of the debates of the legislature and show that there was any mis-statement in regard to all this or any concealment in the statements presented to the legislature. I wish to point out another fact which will show the unfairness of these commissioners and the absence of a desire on their part to do justice. These commissioners say that the legislation was altered from time to time and that we were given power to issue bonds to a greater extent than the legislature gave us in the first instance. That is true. But is that the business of these commissioners to inquire into? Have they the right to set themselves up against and above the legislature of New Brunswick and to say that the legislature had no right to pass statutes modifying the original legislation? I never before heard that commissioners had the right to do that. I never heard that these commissioners were appointed for the purpose of questioning the policy of the legislature. I never understood that and I do not think anybody else ever did. But what these commissioners say is: It is true that by statute the legislature in 1904 made a change in the original legislation and authorized the granting of the whole issue of bonds upon and in respect of the new line and its branches without making a provision for a coal plant and without making certain provision for the building of the line through to Gibson. And then, at page 19 of the report the commissioners say:
After this the Act of 1904 was passed and an obscure section introduced which allowed the government to guarantee bonds for any section of the road to a greater proportion, and so on.
Well, Mr. Powell says this obscure section

1 beg pardon Judge Landry says:
This obscure section was put in the Act of 1904, which allowed us to do just what we did do, but these commissioners say that the members of the legislature who consented to it could hardly have understood that they were giving authority to the government to guarantee the whole issue of $450,000 of bonds. And this is one of the grounds of attack which they made on us: That we guaranteed the whole $450,000 of bonds without having a mining plant and without having the road built to Fredericton. In another part of the report they condemn us most strongly for that and they say we were guilty of a great breach of our obligations to the public, and yet on page 19 they say we were fully and completely authorized by the legislature to do exactly what we did, but that the members of the legislature could not have understood what was the effect of the statute. They speak of it as an obscure section. Well, Mr. Speaker, in 1904, when his Bill was introduced, we fully explained to the legis-

lature the situation of affairs. We explained to them the fact that whereas in the first instance we had entered into a contract which we supposed would have enabled the road to have been completed right through from Chipman to Fredericton or to Gibson, that owing to the difficulties of construction being greater than anticipated, owing to it becoming necessary to take the work off the hands of the contractor, that the company would not be able to establish a mining plant and that these bonds might all have to be used in connection with the 15 mile section and the branches and the repairs and improvements which were being made to the Central. We stated that fully to the House and if hon. gentlemen will look through the discussions which took place in 1904 they will find that one of the points which were made against us by Mr. Hazen, then the leader of the opposition, was that we were providing by this Bill so that the whole issue of bonds might be used and so that there would not be sufficient bonds left for the purpose of carrying the road right through to Fredericton. And yet these commissioners say that was an obscure section which the members of the legislature could not have understood. As against that statement I present the fact, which any hon. gentleman can see for himself, that in the discussions in 1904 in the legislature this very point was raised by the leader of the opposition, and that the premier of the province at the time explained what was the effect and the intention of the Act. And the legislature in full knowledge of what these provisions of the Act were, passed the Bill authorizing the government to do exactly what was done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Was the minister going to read a statement of Mr. Hazen?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I had intended to but I could not find it at the moment. I have it now. At page 169 this discussion is reported :
Hon Mr. Tweedie,-When this company-started it was intended that they should establish a mining plant and they made every afford to obtain one. Their attention was directed to the Bntler elevator, which operated on what was termed the land dredging system. Mr. Butler visited the mines, but they were unable to come to terms with him. Mr. Butler would not sell his machine, which was valued at $150,000, but demanded a dollar and ten cents for every ton of coal mined. He also wanted a straight run of half a mile or a mile for the machine to operate in. It was discovered that the seams did not run so as to admit of this. It was then thought best to build branch lines to the mines that were already in operation. A line five miles in length was built to the Gibbon mine and it also served several other mines. A shorter line was built to Senator King s mine. There was no doubt as to the success of the mining operations in Queens county,
but the road had only been opened a short time and its possibilities had not been developed.
Mr. Hazen stated that the section with regard to the provincial secretary being allowed to guarantee bonds, although the amount of guarantee might be greater than the mileage completed justified, was the most objectionable in the Bill. It appeared that although only 15 miles of the road had been built most of the bonds had been issued so that there would be no funds with which to build the road from Newcastle to Fredericton.
There you have the statement made by the government that the idea of building the mining plant had been abandoned, that it had been thought better to build branch lines into the various operating mines and to encourage the existing mine owners and and you find the statement made by Mr. Hazen, the leader of the opposition, in criticism of this 'obscure' section, that it did just what we told the legislature it would do and what the commissioners admit in their report it authorized us to do. And you find also that not only Mr. Hazen but all the members of the legislature were fully informed of the necessity which had arisen to make the guarantee of bonds which had been made, and also of the desirability of abandoning the policy of establishing a mining plant and building branch lines to the various mines in order to encourage the exsting mine owners and in order to induce the development of other mines. Then I am going to cite another statement to show the reckless character of the report of these commissioners. This will be number six or numbeT seven ; I have about fourteen more before I get through. On page 71, referring to this Act of 1904, they say :
Before this provision was enacted, perhaps in anticipation of it, the whole issue of $450,000 bonds was out and had been nearly all, if not absolutely all, guaranteed and used.
And yet. in another part of the report they state that in June 1904, months after this statute had been passed which authorized the additional guarantee, this company had put into the Bank of New Brunswick $52,500 bonds, and received on these bonds an absolutely new loan, and those bonds were not guaranteed until after the statute of 1904 had been passed which fully authorized the guarantee to be made. There you find two utterly different statements on different pages of this report, showing either that the report was drawn by two different people and that the different parts of it had not been compared, or the utter recklessness of the statements which these commissioners made.
Let me speak of another matter to show the great length to which these commissioners have gone in their desire to make an attack upon the members of the late



government. At page 29 they say with regard to Lieut.-Gov. Tweedie:
It will be noted that Hon. Mr. Tweedie retained one per cent commission, $500 on the sale of $50,000 bonds made by him in Chatham.
Let me explain the circumstances of that. Mr. Tweedie was Provincial Secretary, but he was doing what the members of the government of New Brunswick did then, did before his time, and do to-day-he was practicing his profession. The Hon. Mr. Blair continued the practice of his profession while he was in the government, Mr. Tweedie continued his, I continued mine, Mr. Hazen continued his, and until the province pays larger salaries-I believe our successors have made a move in that direction, although they have not been very long in office-the members of the government will continue to practise their professions. Mr. Tweedie was at that time practising law in the town of Chatham in the county of Northumberland. This company had issued those bonds some months before the transactions which these commissioners refer to took place. They had got a loan from the Bank of New Brunswick on which they were paying 6i or 7 per cent interest, as these commissioners state. The company were desirous, if possible, of getting a loan on the bonds at a lower rate of interest, so as to save all the interest possible; but they did not want to sell the bonds, because at that time it was expected that the Grand Trunk Pacific would come through the town of Chipman, and that this road would form a junction with the Transcontinental at Chipman, as has actually taken place since, and they wanted to keep control of the bonds, so that in the future, if it was thought better, this railway might amalgamate with or be absorbed by or be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the bond issue might be cancelled and the liability of the government wiped out, and in that way the province be freed from this guarantee. Mr. Tweedie had a client, Mr. Hickson, living at Miramichi; my hon. friend from Northumberland probably knows him very well. Mr. Tweedie learned that he was anxious to make an investment in good securities, and he saw him and made an arrangement with him under which he took $50,000 of those bonds which were then held by the Bank of New Brunswick as collateral for a discount. Mr. Hickson took the bonds at par, they bearing interest at 4 per cent, and gave to the company an agreement that if at any time within five years they wished to redeem the bonds, they could do so on paying par and 5 per cent premium. This was an exceedingly good arrangement for the company. It at once saved them the heavy interest by from 2 to 2i per cent, and was to Mr. PUGSLEY.
all intents and purposes a loan, because of the right the company had to redeem the bonds at any time within five years by paying 5 per cent premium. And what do you think is the crime with which Mr. Tweedie is charged and which these commissioners cannot condone? That in making that sale of bonds he charged a commission of 1 per cent, amounting to $500, and did it with the approval of the executive committee of the company. It was done openly and aboveboard. If it had been done by brokers, the company would probably have had to pay a commission of 2 or 2i per cent, He made an excellent arrangement for the company, and the company gladly allowed him that commission on the sale, which was executed at his law office in Chatham. This is what the commissioners say:
This much must be fairly said of this transaction, namely, that Mr. Tweedie sold $50,000 bonds in October, 1903, at par, which was 2h per cent more than the price received from Messrs. Robinson & Sons, who purchased $368,000 of the company's bonds in March, 1905, at 97i, and 5 per cent more than was received by Mr. McAvity, president, for $8,000 of the same bonds.
They further say:
Mr. Tweedie also promptly accounted for the accrued interest, $575.34, which in other oases we consider is not accounted for. Without condoning this transaction, we think, on the whole, it is amenable to less censure than others spoken of in this report. It at least has the merit when it did come to light of being clear cut and definite, without any effort being made to conceal it from your commissioners.
What would you infer from that? Would you not infer that in some way those commissioners had brought that matter to light, and that when they had done so Mr. Tweedie had accounted for the interest, which was something others had not done. Sir, the bringing of it to light was this. When Mr. Tweedie was on the stand he was asked in regard to the sale of these bonds, and he replied:	'You will find a
full statement in the Bank of New Brunswick'; and he went to the bank and brought up a statement showing that four years before that time he had obtained from Mr. Hickson $50,575.34, being the principal and the accrued interest on the bonds, he had deducted his $500 of commission, and had then sent a cheque for $50,075.34 to the Bank of New Brunswick. And yet these commissioners speak of this as if he had accounted for it only when they brought it to light.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is that not what the commissioners say?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I think it is not. I think the fair inference to be drawn from their report is that it had come to light

before them, and that then Mr. Tweedie had accounted for the interest. So far from his accounting for it then, he had accounted for it to the company four years before and had accounted for it in the proper way. The whole business was done openly and above board. Yet notwithstanding the fact that this was a purely business transaction, notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Tweedie by this saved the company 24 to 3 per cent in interest, and that the company entirely approved of his commission as reasonable, these commissioners, in their anxiety to say something against Mr. Tweedie, who was formerly provincial secretary, say that without condoning the transaction, on the whole it is amenable to less censure than the others spoken of. There is the statement that these commissioners cannot condone that transaction. There is their statement that this transaction has one thing to commend it and that is that when it came to light, Mr. Tweedie promptly accounted for the interest.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman contend that this phrase means what he says or that Mr. Tweedie promptly accounted at the time he made the sale:
Mr. Tweedie also promptly accounted for the further interest of $575.34, but in another case we consider it was not accounted for.
Does that say he accounted for it at the time?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
One cannot tell, from the phraseology these commissioners use in their report, what they really meant, but it is clear that they endeavoured to convey wrong impressions. I cannot say what they meant when they used these words:
Mr. Tweedie promptly accounted for the further interest of $575.84. Without condoning thi9 transaction, we think, on the whole, it is amenable to less censure than the others spoken of. It has at least the merit, when it ' did come to light, of being clear cut and definite, without any effort being made to conceal it from your commissioners.
I appeal to the House if it is not a fair inference that this was something which had been concealed, but which, through the probing of these commissioners into the depths of everything, had come to light; that then Mr. Tweedie had promptly accounted for the interest, and in that respect he was better than the others.
At six o'clock the House took recess. After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before recess I was pointing out some statements contained in the report, which statements 1804
show how little reliance is to be placed upon this report. I am doing this without troubling the House by referring to the evidence. I may say that I could not refer to the evidence even if I desired to do so, because I have not been able to obtain a full copy. I have copies of, I think, two volumes, but have not been able to obtain the rest, because, though this report states (that the commissioners transmit to the provincial ^secretary the evidence, as a part of the report, yet the evidence has not been printed although request that it should be printed was made in the provincial legislature. Of course, it would be quite impossible, even if there were a copy of the evidence here, for hon. gentlemen who are called upon to base their opinion upon this report to form an intelligent judgment upon the evidence without having an opportunity of carefully perusing it. Therefore it is that I am limiting my observations mainly to the report itself. I was giving a number of examples of contradictory statements contained in the report which fairly show that portions of it are false. As evidence of the unfairness and carelessness of these commissioners, I wish to call your attention to the fact that in attempting to disparage and depreciate the value of the Central Railway, the part of the road between Norton and Chipman built some years ago, before the new road was undertaken, the commissioners say, at page 19 of the report:
The province has obtained, net forty odd miles, but fifteen miles of railway, a few cheap sidings, a quantity of rolling stock costing between twenty and thiity tnousand dollars.
Now, Sir, in the report itself it appears that the new rolling stock purchased by the company amounted to $26,000. The report shows also, at page 74, that there has been purchased additional new rolling stock to the amount of $23,779.88; These two items together make over $53,000 worth of new rolling stock, and this is addition to the rolling stock obtained as part of the purchase of the Central Railway. I doubt very much whether the $23,779 is correct, for the reason that the report of the Auditor General of the province of New Brunswick for 1907 states the new rolling stock at something over $30,000. But assuming that it is only $23,779, as this report states, you have there with all the rolling stock upon the road worth, including what was purchased as part of the Central, $78,500

a road fairly equipped with rolling stock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Where is the other
item?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
That is what was taken over as part of the Central. It may appear in one of the documents, and not in the report. In another reference, these commissioners speak of the promoters' stock. My

hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) has referred to that as evidence of a typewritten error in the report, to which very little attention should be paid. It can hardly be a typewritten error in the ordinary sense, because it is this printed report which is signed by the commissioners, filed with the provincial secretary and presented to the legislature as the report of these commissioners. That this report was gone over by the commissioners before they signed it and after it was printed is shown by the fact that they were careful to insert at the very beginning certain errata. For instance:
Page 55, 26th line: outside of the Salmon Eiver bridge, there are, &c., ' 60' instead of * 50.'
Page 55, 38th line: * company's engineers ' instead of ' provincial engineers.'
Page 55, 19th line, insert: 'as was intimated ' after the words ' it is not.'
These are the only errors which they corrected in this printed report before they signed it. They did not sign a typewritten copy, but they signed the printed report, and that is filed as the report of the commission. And on page 63 these commissioners seek to magnify the importance of the large amount of stock which is being distributed among the promoters, because they use this language-the language of exaggeration, calculated to throw ridicule upon the promoters, and show that they had visions of great wealth from the distribution of this large amount of stock:
On the face of it the motive of the promoters as stated was to develop tHe c'rl mines of Queens county. Responsible and respectable men from various parts of the province were obtained to lend their names as directors; and from the fact that $130,003 of the total $500,000 authorized capital was [DOT]to be distributed as founders' shares, we conclude that the interested parties had visions of ultimate large profits, with absolute certainty of no personal loss.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Does the hon minister (Mr. Pugsley) think that was a deliberate mis-statement?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I have seen so many mis-statements in this report that it is hard for me to distinguish those which are deliberate and those which are the result of mistakes. I cannot imagine men of fairness, men exercising sound judgment, men desirous of simply stating facts, putting forward the statements which are contained in this report. Why did they ignore evidence on this point? These commissioners had it in evidence, in the testimony of Mr. Skinner, that, after this company was formed, those who were interested in the company started in to organize the company for the development of the coal mines, and they made a change with regard to any distribution of this stock and that these shares were handed over to Judge Trueman by Mr. Skinner to hold Mr. PUGSLEY.
in trust for the company. And, Sir, the statement was made, in the legislature, in answer to a question put by the leader of the opposition there, that this stock was held in trust for the company with the exception of a few shares which were sold to raise money in connection with the preliminary work looking toward the development of the coal mines. And what would you expect under those circumstances? Although Judge Trueman has passed away, would you not expect that in his safe, among his private and confidential papers, there would be found those shares of stock handed to him in trust for the company? And yet, Sir, so afraid were these commissioners that they would discover some of the truth in regard to these shares which would prevent the-suspicion going abroad that they had been delivered over for the benefit possibly of members of the government, that they never called one of Judge Trueman's executors to show whether or not this stock was there in his safe and from statements which Judge Trueman made to me in his lifetime I have not the shadow of a doubt that these shares of stock, whenever the examination takes place, if it does take place, will be found among his papers 'in the place where, being entrusted to him, it would be expected they would be found. In this connection I shall speak of one other matter. It was shown that by the order of the 6th August, 1903, bonds of this company, guaranteed, were handed over to Judge Trueman for the purpose of completing the title to the Central Railway, because, as I am going to explain to you, Evans and Elkin were not able to complete the title for the reason that they only owned the bonds and a portion of the stock, there being something like $300,000 of par value stock outstanding. They were aware that a quantity of the bonds were handed to Judge Trueman, in order that he and Mr. Allen might complete the title to the property, and these commissioners never made the slightest inquiry under oath, never called any one connected with Judge Trueman's estate, to ascertain whether or not there was a record of these bonds. What is the explanation they give of this? That having made some inquiry they believed there would be no advantage in having any testimony before them so far as the late Judge Trueman was concerned. Judge Trueman was a man of the highest integrity, a man occupying a very high and honourable position in St. John, a man who had been for a good many years judge of probates of that city and who at the time of his death, was chairman of the board of school trustees, a man universally respected and on whose honour and integrity every one would have the most implicit reliance. When these bonds were entrusted to him, to have the title to the

Central Kailway completed, we all knew that he would faithfully and honourably discharge the trust and when later on it was reported to Mr. Sharpe, the auditor, that it had cost the company the amount of the original option, the amount which the company was bound to pay to Evans and Elkin or to whoever should be entrusted with the money in order to complete the title, Mr. Sharpe believed and rightly believed and we all had the right to believe that the sum which it was agreed in the first place should be paid for the Central Kailway was actually paid to complete the title and that sum was $180,000. Yet, although the commissioners in this report seek to throw discredit upon the conduct generally of the officers of the company, they did not think it worth while to make any inquiry under oath as to what documents there were in Judge Trueman's possession or what record there was in his possession in respect to these bonds or any other matters connected with the New Brunswick coal and Railway Company.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Unfortunately I came in late and I wish to understand the hon. gentleman clearly. Do I understand that he has been speaking of the 4,300 shares of stock which, according to the report of the commission

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: My hon. friend is a thousand per eeht out of the way, it is only 430 shares.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: We understand there is a typographical mistake such as is sometimes made even by ministers. It is of that stock, however, that I am inquiring. Am I right in understanding that that much is reported as having been, per minute of the directors, handed over to Judge Trueman, and with reference to the shortage of the $180,000 for the purchase of the Central Railway that about $40,000 of those bonds were handed over to Judge Trueman to complete the title? Is that the statement my hon. friend makes?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I will repeat my statement in order that there will be no misunderstanding. It appears from the evidence of Mr. Skinner that there had been a change in the plans of the company; it was proposed to form a coal mining company and Mr. Skinner had delivered to Judge Trueman this stock which had been issued to him, some 430 shares. It was stated in the legislature, as will appear from the synoptic reports in an answer to a question put to me, that that stock was for the benefit of the company and, as I have said, I have not a shadow of doubt that if the executors of Judge Trueman had been called and had been asked to look into the strong box where he
kept private documents, that stock would have been found there. I assume it would, it ought to be. These commissioners, notwithstanding that Mr. Skinner said that he had handed mat stock to Judge Trueman, and notwithstanding that there was in evidence before them the order given to the manager. of the Royal Trust Company on the 6th of August, 1903, when the title to the Central Railway was being completed, bonds to enable him to complete the title to the Central Railway, the commissioners did not call representatives of Judge Trueman's estate and they gave no explanation as to their not calling them beyond the fact that on making inquiry they had been led to believe there would be no advantage in calling such representatives.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Does the minister mean that the bonds were handed over to Judge Trueman to acquire the balance of the stock of the Central Railway?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: To complete the title to the Central Railway.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: When the minister says to complete the title, does he mean to acquire the balance of the stock?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Not at all, to complete the title; whatever was necessary to complete the title Judge Trueman was entrusted with.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: What was necessary?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: All things necessary. During the progress of events the minority shareholders, so it was reported, claimed that these bondholders in Philadelphia were not the actual owners of these bonds, but that they had loaned money on them and that they were in the position of mortgagees in possession and objected to Evans and Elkin getting the whole amount of the $180,000 less what would be going to the American bondholders, and the evidence is that Messrs. Evans and Elkin, or Mr. Evans, engaged with Messrs. Allen and Trueman that anything reasonable which was necessary to quiet the minority shareholders and prevent any objection being made to enable them to get the title, they were authorized to do, and Evans and Elkin finally settled with them taking themselves a less amount by some $38,000 than what the original agreement and option provided for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman said he had not all the evidence here but does he say that Mr. Evans gives evidence to the effect that they were at liberty to hand

over stock to satisfy the Central Railway Company in the way the minister indicates?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The evidence is that they were authorized to use part of the purchase money to complete the title.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I have never found that in the evidence although I have read it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: That is my recollection of the evidence and as a matter of fact we have it in evidence that on one occasion, when Mr. Evans gave to the company a receipt for $60,000, being for the first four payments of $15,000 each, there was a deduction made by Mr. Allen pursuant to an arrangement they had, proportionate to the amount. That is in evidence and is referred to in the report. I will refer to that later. All I speak of now is that these bonds were used, and I have no doubt legitimately and properly and honestly used, for the purpose of acquiring the title. Evans and Elkins were not the owners of the Central Railway. They only had two-thirds of stock and the bonds and therefore, in order to procure the title and carry out their agreement to sell they would, unless the minority shareholders were willing, have been obliged to have taken foreclosure proceedings and my hon. friends opposite, especially those in the legal profession, will understand what it means when a mortgagee in possession undertakes to foreclose as against a minority interest. It would have taken months and perhaps years, there might have been protracted legal proceedings and they were quite willing to make an arrangement with Messrs. Allen and Trueman to satisfy the minority shareholders and to get a perfect title, and it was done in that way without the expense and delay of foreclosure proceedings.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: At what time did Mr. Trueman die?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend just at this moment. It would be, I think, two years ago. Now, I will show you another instance

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Did the minister, as representing New Brunswick and as being a member of the company as well, convince himself by seeing the documents and knowing exactly what had been done, that the title had been cleared?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Yes, that the title had been completed. There was a certificate to that effect.
meantime, $540,000 of bonds were held as security until the deeds were recorded and the title was. completed. Messrs. Evans & Elkins agreed to give it, but they were not in a position to give it without the concurrence of the other shareholders. As another evidence of the recklessness of these commissioners, of the want of care, it will be found, at page 25 of this report, that they make this statement:
Large sums of money, amounting in all to $190,873.04, were from time to time expended it is alleged for improvements on the Central railway between July, 1902, and March 31, 1908; and on the fifteen mile section and branches from July 1, 1904, to March 31, 1908.
This is an allegation that a large amount of money was expended in improvements on the Central Railway, and the conclusion is sought to be drawn that the road could not have been originally worth as much as was given for it. Well, if you turn to page 74 you will find that out of an expenditure of $190,873.04 the large sum of $23,779.88 went for absolutely new rolling stock. Yet, in another part of this report they say that the whole of it was for improvements made upon the railway. I call attention to it as an evidence of the utter carelessness with which these commissioners apparently have had this report made up and have put it forward as a report of the facts when it is a report of everything else but the facts.
Then, I come to what is even worse. Take page 14 of this report. This is a dreadful statement to make. It is a strong indictment:
So much of the facts are given to show the absolute want of book-keeping.
What would be taken from that? Is it not that there was shown a total want of book-keeping, that there was no attempt to keep a record of the expenditures of this company? Then, again on another page of the report you will see that they state it was claimed that the Barnes Construction Company kept books, but that they were destroyed and not produced before these commissioners. Well, Sir, if you turn to another part of this report you will find that they are speaking of the reliability of Mr. Shannon's statement as to the interest and as to the cost of the construction of this road. They say, at page 22, that Mr. Shannon

had the benefit of Mr. Evans' statement,
the books of the James Barnes Construction Company
and of all information that he could derive from Mr. Sharpe, the company's auditor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: From whom?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
From Mr. Trueman or Mr. Skinner. The title was searched, .everything was completed and, in the Mr. LENNOX.
There, they put forward the positive statement that Mr. Shannon had the benefit of the books of the James Barnes Construction Company, which they had not, and on another page they state that it was

claimed that the James Barnes Company kept books, but that they were destroyed, casting a doubt upon the sworn testimony of James Barnes that they had books, that the work being done, the accounts being closed, the business being off his hands four years before this investigation took place, they were either lost or destroyed, because he had no further use for them, and, in another page of that report, stating positively, as we all know was the fact, that Mr. Shannon had had the advantage of going carefully over the books of the James Barnes Construction Company. An absolute want of bookkeeping, say they! Turn to page 8 of this report and compare this statement that there was an absolute want of bookkeeping with what you find there.
Books of account

They say:

in connection with the operation of the
railway were kept in the company's otiioe at Norton. These books besides showing the revenue and operating expenses, show the amounts expended for betterment outside of the cost of the construction of the fifteen mile section and branches, and were well kept.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman satisfied that he is putting that fairly?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Yes, absolutely word for word as the report gives it. Then turn again, Sir, to the statement of the cost of this new railway. These commissioners sent out their emissaries in all directions, issued their subpoenas to the officers, to Mr. Barnes, to Mr. Evans, to Mr. Fowler, the clerks at Norton and others, and, Sir, after it is all over, what do they do? They adopt absolutely the statement of Mr. Evans, the chief engineer and the manager of the company at Norton, as to the cost of the fifteen-mile section and branches Let me read what they say at page 21 in regard to it. After they had spent months and months endeavouring to find out what this road cost, hoping that they would be able to throw some discredit upon somebody connected with the government, or some friend of the government in connection with these matters, what do they say?
Mr. Evans' statement of cost is a very methodical and comprehensive one. He places the cost of the fifteen mile section and branches at $316,626.33, the figures which we have adopted.
Even down to the 33 cents. Who was Mr. Evans? He was the chief engineer and general manager of the company. He was looking after the office at Norton, where was situated the great spending department of the company and where it was proper that the accounts should be kept. We had presented to the legislature in March, 1904, a statement of cost down to March 31, 1904, being $321,000 or just $5,000 more than Mr. Evans made it on the 1st of January, 1904.
These commissioners, in the end, after all their inquiry for months, adopt Mr. Evans' statement as being the correct statement of the cost of the fifteen miles and branches. They say there was no book-keeping. How did Mr. Evans arrive at that statement. It was not made for this examination; it was made four years ago, it was submitted to the government and to the legislature at that time as being the correct cost of the new line and of the branches. I want to say, Sir, that from month to month dur* ing all the time that this work was in pro^ gress Mr. Evans as chief engineer furnished to the company and to myself as representing the government, a full and detailed statement of the cost, made up minutely as engineers of railway companies make up such statements, and we knew from month to month exactly what that road was costing. These statements of Mr. Evans were placed on file in the office of the executive council and I have a sample copy here which if any gentleman chooses to examine he will see is in minute detail. It seems to me to be a refutation of the statement that there was an absolute lack of bookkeeping. There were the books of the James Barnes Construction Company kept while they were working as contractors and also while they were carrying on the work under the force arrangement with their percentage added, and there were books, as the commission admits, at Norton, showing all the receipts and the expenditure of the road, and all the improvements made on the road amounting to many thousands of dollars. The statement of Mr. Evans, the company's chief engineer and general manager, the commission say, is a most methodical and comprehensive one, and they adopt that to the very last cent as being a correct statement of the cost of the construction of the 15 miles and branches.

There are five gentlemen who were prominently connected with the company and all of whom have died since the road was completed. And these commissioners rather put that forward as if it were almost our fault and as if we ought to account for what was done or ought to have done by these gentlemen in their lifetime.
Now, Sir, what we did so far as bookkeeping was concerned at the start' in the way of organization was this: In the first place we had an examination made of the coal areas; we sent a committee of council there to look into the existing coal mines and we got that committee to inquire into possible markets. Communications were opened up with Mr. Blair who was then Minister of Railways and we informed him that we were about developing these coal areas if it were possible to do so and if we thought we would be justified in the attempt. Many attempts had been made in that direction in the .past, but because of the expensive nature of the work to get from Chipman to Minto it had not been found possible to make this extension, and here were lying close to the surface and capable of being easily mined these vast undeveloped deposits of coal estimated at about 100, 000,000 tons and belonging to the province. We opened up communications with Mr. Blair as I have said, and we asked him if the railroad were built whether he would undertake that the Intercolonial Railway should use a certain quantity of the coal per year. I have in my possession a letter from Mr. Blair which I am quite willing that anybody should see and he as Minister of Railways states that as soon as the road was finished, which it was contemplated would be early the next year, the government would take for the Intercolonial Railway 30,000 tons of coal provided it was of good quality and the price was reasonable, and further, that under these conditions the company might calculate upon a sale to the Intercolonial Railway of about 60,000 tons per year. That in itself opened up good prospects for the company. It would give a good traffic at about 60 cents per ton amounting to $36,000 per year, and it would give to the province a royalty of 10 cents per ton. Then, inquiry was made among the manufacturers who had been using this coal and it was found that it had been highly approved of and that a large market could be expected in St. John. Something has been said about the fact that the gentlemen who went into the company did not put any of their own money into it. Well, Sir, I state frankly-and it was so stated to the legislature and to the people

in 1901, and we had a general election since and the people approved of out efforts to develop these coal areas-it was never understood that these gentlemen should put their own money into it. It is exactly like the ease of a company which was incorporated by the New Brunswick legislature the other day for the purpose of endeavouring to procure the construction of a railway down the valley of the St. John. People upon both sides of politics united for the purpose of forming a company to build that line in order to give accommodation to the people. It is not understood, it never is understood in cases of this kind that those people are going to put their own money into such an undertaking. These gentlemen were got together; men as the report says of high standing, men of integrity, men who patriotically desired to see these coal areas developed associated themselves in this company. I should also say that an arrangement was made with Mr. Blair at that time to get rails from the Dominion government which were to be paid for in coal from time to time. We believed that having made that arrangement we would be able, with guaranteed bonds amounting to $250,000, to secure the construction of the railway between Chipman and Fredericton. The estimates of the engineers showed there would be sufficient margin for this purpose and also to provide a small amount of rolling stock. Then the question was as to how this company could finance in the meantime, because under the terms of the legislation which we first proposed in 1901 and which was agreed to, none of these bonds were to be guaranteed until the whole road was completed. We felt at the time that even with that condition, hard though it was, the road could be completed. The James Barnes Construction Company put in a tender for the first 15 miles and there was another tender from Mr. Wheaton for the same section. Mr. Wheaton's tender was a little less than the tender of Mr. Barnes and I observe that a strong reflection is made upon the company, and made I suppose indirectlv upon myself as ex officio member of the company, because we consented to allow Mr. Wheaton to withdraw and gave the contract to the next tender, the James Barnes Construction Company.
If I had been consulted-I do not remember whether I was or riot, but very likely I was-I will tell you why I would have approved of giving the contract to the James Barnes Construction Company instead of to Mr. Wheaton. Mr. Wheaton was a contractor of considerable experience, it is true; but he had failed in railway construction work. He was without means, and it would have been utterly impossible for him to have carried on that work unless he was paid from month to month on pro-

Therefore, as be-ween the two contractors there is no question that the proper thing was to accept the tender of the James Barnes Construction Company, although it was $4,000 or $5,000 higher than that of Mr. Wheaton. And yet, apparently, without knowledge of the circumstances, these commissioners put that forward as a most reprehensible thing to do, and attribute the difficulties which occurred afterwards in large measure to the fact that the contract was given to the James Barnes Construction Company instead of to Mr. Wheaton. Before I go to another part of the case, I would like to state what was the arrangement with regard to financing of the company and the way in which the road was to be built. As I have said, Mr. Evans-an engineer of considerable experience and of great ability and on whose report these commissioners placed reliance, because they adopted it so far as the cost is concerned-was in charge at Norton. Norton was the headquarters of the expending department in the way of construction work. Then it was arranged that all the financing was to be done at the People's Bank in Fredericton. From time to time, as the estimates of the engineer would be sent in, there would be a percentage deducted from the progress estimates, the company would give its note to the contractors, the contractors would have that note endorsed by Senator Thompson and Mr. Whitehead and discounted by the bank, and the proceeds would be taken by the constructing company. That is the way the thing was organized, and I think every one will admit that was a proper way, so far as the construction of the road was concerned. The business went on in that way for a considerable time. Mr. Geo. W. Allen was the secretary of the company. It was his duty to perform the ordinary work of a secretary. That was what he was paid for doing and what he was expected to do, and it is what, I cannot help believing, he did do. Mr: Allen was a good business man against whom nobody so far has said a word impeaching his integrity, and he would understand thoroughly what were his duties. He was in every respect well adapted for his position. From time to time Mr. Allen would receive these estimates, he would deduct the ten per cent and give the notes to the company, which would be signed by the treasurer and president or vice-president, and then given to the construction company, and that company would have them discounted. Then there came a time when it was necessary to obtain moneys elsewhere because the People's bank did not feel that it could continue to make advances very much beyond what

speechtext:
were already made. The company therefore did some financing elsewhere. It will be found from the report of the commissioners that a loan was effected with the Bank of Montreal in Fredericton and another with the Bank of British North America in the same place. There is one peculiarity in the report of the commissioners. They make the statement that they cannot trace the moneys which were the proceeds of these notes discounted at the Bank of Montreal ar*d the Bank of British North America, because, they say, these notes were not placed to the company's credit but were drawn out on discount slips. They do not say who signed those slips, but they leave it to be inferred that possibly myself or Mr. Tweedie, as the other member ex-officio of the government, may have negotiated these loans. I presume however that they looked at the discount slips and that they saw that these loans wrere negotiated and those discount slips signed by G. W. Allen, the secretarv of the company. Yet these commissioners do not say so. They do not say who signed the discount slips, but lead the people to infer, according as might be their feelings and desires, who got the proceeds. But would it not have been fair and honourable for the commissioners to have said that they had seen the discount slips and that these slips were signed by
G.	W. Allen, the secretary of the company, which fact would trace the money directly to the company through its secretary? When I read the report and saw that extraordinary omission, I thought that these commissioners and their counsel wanted to throw out the inuendo that possibly Mr. Pugsleiy had to do with the negotiation of these loans, and that possibly the proceeds may have gone into his hands, which might go far to accomplish the mission with which they had started out, and that was to make a report strong enough to compel me to leave the government. Afterwards notes were discounted at the Bank of New Brunswick in the city of St. John and loans were also obtained from the Canada Permanent.
I want to refer, just for a moment longer, to Mr. Allen. I assume that he kept a memorandum of the notes given by the company from time to time. I assume that he kept a memorandum of all the checks he gave when the notes were placed to the company's credit, and that the check stubs, or the checks themselves, would show to whose order the moneys were payable, because he was not in the habit of paying out money except by cheque. And I assume also that he kept a cash-book or memorandum which would show the discounts from time to time. Well, these commissioners say that they could get no evidence of what these cheques were given for, so far as the banks at Fredericton are con-

cerned, because, they say, the banks gave up the cheques. But if they did, they must have given them up in the ordinary course to Mr. Allen, the secretary fo the company. There is nothing suspicious in a bank giving up its cheques. The banks always give them up each month when the credit or debit slip, as the case may be, is signed. Yet the fact is put forward as if it were something suspicious that these cheques were given up by the banks. When the late Mr. Sharpe was appointed accountant to audit these books and accounts, I know that the cheques in the banks in St. John were, by direction, handed over to him, and I assume that all the cheques on the banks in Fredericton were handed over to the auditor by Mr. Allen, the secretary, iand that the stubs and everything which would let in light on the accounts would be given to him, -including any memorandum or cash-books which the secretary of the company might have. After the lapse of years, and these accounts and books had not been got back from Mr. Sharpe, who unfortunately died just as he was completing his work, but who fortunately submitted an audit just before he died, because these cheques and Mr. Barnes books had not been got back, these commissioners sought to draw inferences against those of us who had to do with the formation of the company. I said, and the commissioners ridiculed the statement, that an accountant, sincerely desirous of getting at the facts of the case, could in two or three days make up a complete statement of the receipts and expenditures of that company. I am the more confirmed in that statement, the more I read the report of the commissioners. Because they say that at Norton there was a complete account of all receipts and expenditures so far as the betterment of the road and the operation of the road were concerned. They adopt finally the statement of Mr. Evans, manager and engineer of the road, and say that his statement is comprehensive and methodical. They eopld go to the Bank of New Brunswick, the Canada Permanent-and it appears they did have both of these before them-the People's Bank, the Bank of British North America, and the Bank of Montreal, and get a statement of the discounts put through from time to time the proceeds of which went to the company's credit or were drawn out by discount slips. In that way, they could get with almost absolute accuracy the interest accruing from 1901 to 1908. That is the statement I made before the commissioners and that is the statement I adhere to. I am sorry, not so much for my own sake as for the sake of these commissioners, that they did not think it worth while, with all the machinery, they had at their command, to endeavour to arrive
with some degree of accuracy at the amount of interest, but jumped at it in the way I have spoken of. When this report came out stating that the interest was $92,000, I thought it might be well to have an inquiry made in the legislature as to how that interest was made up, because I took it for granted that the commissioners, particularly when one was a judge, would be in a position to furnish all the details. I do not want to contradict the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) who says that this gentleman is an eminent judge, if he knows. But if any hon. gentleman were to tell me that Judge Landry, when appointed to the bench, was specially selected for his great eminence in his profession, I should feel that he had but little knowledge of the transaction of legal business in the province of New Brunswick and but little knowledge of the leading counsel who in the past have appeared before the various courts in that _ province. He is a judge as other judges are, but that he is specially eminent I am not prepared to admit. I am not here to-night to disparage Mr. Justice Landry. I have great respect for the bench, but I have more respect for those judges who uphold the dignity and honour of the bench, and I like to see them endeavouring to do that. I like to see them, when they go upon the bench, forget that they have been in political life, but I hate to see a judge, when a general election is coining on, begin to coquet with one of the great political parties with regard to his becoming a candidate, of the party. It tends to prevent his mind from settling down to that judicial calm which is necessary to enable one to adorn the high position of a judge. With regard to the other commissioners, I have but little to say. Mr. Macdougall has been a manager of a branch of the Royal Bank. He has been for a good while manager of a branch, and a not very important branch either. It has been his misfortune to see men younger, far younger, who have been appointed to minor and inferior positions long after he went there, passing on over him to higher positions in that great institution. He is a man who, for many years, while Mr. Powell was engaged in his profession in Westmoreland .county was engaged with Mr. Powell in business transactions, particularly with regard to one manufacturing company. It is a somewhat curious fact that, in selecting this commission, they did not look to the chief justice of the Supreme Court, they did not look to any gentleman who had been a Liberal before he had been appointed to the bench. They were careful to see to it that the three members of this commission should be good solid Tories,-at least that one of them, before appointment to the bench,

had been a good solid Tory and the other two should be such at this time. They were careful to see, also, that the counsel to guide them with regard to the evidence brought before them and to assist them in making up this report should be Mr. H. A. Powell, who has been a member of this House and has been a candidate in the Conservative interest in a good many contests in the province of New Brunswick, in not all of which he was successful in being returned to parliament. While this is the case, I am not of the opinion that I should bow down to and worship any member of this commission or give any undue respect to the report, but that I should only give to it that respect which the report upon its face seems to deserve. Now, as I was saying, when this statement was made of interest of $92,000, and when there was no statement as to how it was made up, and when we found other items put in in the lump and financial matters divided up in such a way that no person could tell from the report whether there had been left out large or small sums in the way of disbursements, I suggested to a friend of mine in the legislature that a question should be put to the government with regard to the interest-this amount of $92,000-how it was made up, to what banks it had been paid, what rate of interest had been charged, and also whether it was compounded. I took it for granted that these commissioners, while they only put summaries into the report, would have statements which could be readily furnished to the government, showing the way in which this amount had been arrived at. And this was the answer given:

It does seem to me that, before the commissioners sent broadcast over this country a statement which, though not charging me with the receipt, improperly, of a single dollar of the money of this company, yet is calculated to cast reflection upon somebody connected with the company as showing carelessness and want of regard to the duties of those who have to do with the company, they should have asked through their accountant the bank managers to make up for them a statement of the interest.
