The improvements necessary to be made by the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company to the Central Railway for the purposes above mentioned will amount approximately to $25,000, of which to first December "$9,852.85 was actually expended. _
It is certainly proper to consider the improvements made to the Central, and more especially those in connection with the terminals at Chipman, in forming a judgment as to what amount of bonds it would be proper to guarantee.
The value of the work done by the present contractor upon the line between Chipman and Newcastle, including the branch to coal mines and engineering expenses during construction to 30th November, 1902, is $74,547.35.
Not $140,000 as these commissioners would have the public believe, but $74,543.35.
Having carefully considered the matter, and keeping in view the work done relatively to that to be done, I think it would be proper for the Provincial Secretary to guarantee bonds of the company on behalf of the province to the amount of $140,000. This amount, however, to include bonds previously guaranteed.	.
In making this estimate I leave out of consideration the amount paid on the purchase money of the Central Railway, although it seems proper to refer to it as above.
There you have a statement giving in minute detail the cost of the work done up to that date upon this line of railway. You have a statement of the cost of the ne|w work, of the bridge at Salmon river, a large and expensive bridge which had been previously bui-lt and had been taken over and had become the property of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company as a part of the purchase of the Central Railway, for which $47,500 had then been paid. You have a statement as to the engineering expenses, as to the cost of the rights of way, but as to the new work the statement was made absolutely, as was the case with the money actually spent up to that time upon the new work, that it was only seventy-four thousand and some odd dollars.
I speak of this in order to show that these commissioners have not hesitated, wherever they could do so, to cast reflections upon the late provincial government. Surely if they wanted fairly to criticise the judg-Mr. PUGSLEY.
ment of the chief engineer in furnishing this report and the judgment of the government in guaranteeing bonds, it would be proper to set these out in detail. But instead of doing that they make a statement which would leave the ordinary reader to believe that the engineer, although there had been only $80,000 of work done upon the railway, had actually represented that work to the extent of $140,000 had then been performed. I mention this as another illustration of the unfairness of this report. I want to call attention to still another matter as showing how thoroughly unreliable are the expressions of opinion which these commissioners give. They speak upon the 56th page of this report of what this new line of railway could have been built for and I mention this for the information of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. I had been urging, the company had been urging, the previous government had been urging that this company should have an increased subsidy because the cost of the road, instead of being $15,000 per mile, had reached $20,000 or $21,000 per mile. Mr. Hazen, the premier of the province, has been urging also that! there should be this increased subsidy, but his commissioners say that this new line, in their judgment, could have been constructed at an average cost of $11,000 per mile. Well, Sir, if Mr. Hazen and his government place any reliance in the estimate that these commissioners have formed as to the value of the road then good-bye to the application of this railway company for an increased subsidy and the provincial government will have to pay for the rails which were obtained from this government and for which it is owing to the Dominion. But, how absurd this is! Did they have an engineer go over the road? No, these commissioners never thought it worth while to get a Tailway engineer to go over this railway to make an examination of it, but, they say, forsooth, in eflect, that Mr. Powell and we went over this road and made an examination of it. Mr. Justice Landry, Mr. Mac-dougall, the manager of a branch bank, Mr. Teed, a small merchant carrying on, business in the town of St. Stephen's and Mr. Powell, a lawyer, going over this railway and estimating its value to be $11,000 per mile! As against that we had the report of one of the most experienced railway engineers in this country who had gone over the road, walked over every foot of it, examined it with the utmost care and he reported that although the rails were lighter than the rails upon the Intercolonial Railway, yet they were of excellent character and in all other respects this road) was built up to the standard of the Intercolonial Railway and was well worth $21,000 per mile. Yet, Sir, havirig a knowledge of that report, because we read it before the

legislature in 1904, and, I think again in 1905, these commissioners, without taking the trouble to have a railway engineer go over this line, coolly put forward in the report, in order to disparage us, the statement that this line, upon the average, is only worth $11,000 per mile. Hon. gentlemen can, from that statement, judge what reliance is to be placed on the opinions, at all events, which these commissioners give.
I want to call your attention to a very unfair statement which occurs upon page 38 of the report. They say:
To make the matter as clear as possible it is necessary to go back to June, 1901, when the first issue of $250,000 3 per cent bonds was made. These bonds being held in various banks for money advanced were replaced by Mr. Shadbolt, of the Royal Trust Company, in August, 1903, with $250,000 of the now total issue of $150,000 1 per cent bonds, leaving a balance of $200,000 which were handed to Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Trueman and afterwards found their way into various banks as security for advances.
I have already shown you, by the order which was given Mr. Shadbolt, the manager of the Royal Trust Company, on the 6th August, 1903, that this statement is false, I have already shown you that the total issue at that time, when the $200,000 of bonds which were isued under the authority of the statute upon completion of the title to the Central Railway, was $338,500 being only $138,500 beyond the $200,000 provided for the purchase of and improvements upon the Central Railway, I have shown you how these bonds were distributed, $70,000 going to the Bank of Montreal in Fredericton, $20,000 going to the Bank of British North America in Fredericton, $27,000 to the Bank of New Brunswick, $70,000 to the Peoples' Bank, who are financing the contractors, $66,000 to the Bank of New Brunswick, which were used for the purpose of taking over the bonds upon the Central and which were then owned by Clark and Company and Drexell, and Company and upon which Messrs. Evans and Elkin held an option and $85,500 which were handed to Judge True man the solicitor of the company for the purposes of the company. Can you place title and the balance to be turned over to Mr. Allen, the secretary, to be used for the purposes of th company. Can you place any reliance upon the report of these commissioners in view of the fact that this order not only gave the amounts of the bonds but gave the numbers of the bonds so that if these moneys or bonds were stolen as suggested, they could easily be identified. Do you think that I, as the Attorney General, would have given to the manager of the Trust Company not only the amounts of these bonds but the numbers of the bonds which were to be handed over to the
various institutions and to the various parties at the time of completion of the title of the Central Railway Company in 1903 if there had been any desire to misapply them in any way? Doing that as I did, these bonds could be traced in any bank in which they were placed because the bank would have on the hypothecation sheet and on the record a statement of the numbers and amounts of the bonds. But, what I complain of is that, having this record before them, having this order at their disposition, they make this general statement that it left $200,000 of bonds which were handed to Mr. Pugsley and Mr. Trueman and afterwards found their way into the various banks as security for advances. The evidence before these commissioners will show that every bond which came into my hands was hypothecated as security for the notes of this company and that the proceeds of these notes were placed to the credit of the company and were checked out by the secretary of the company with the exception of one or two instances when Mr. Barnes, the contractor, at a time when the company was hard up, at a time when it seemed as if they had nobody to turn to except myself, at a time when, owing to delay which was caused by having a thorough audit of the accounts of the company made, they could not get money to pay labour bills, when hundreds of men were clamoring for their wages and when material men were threatening to sue the company, come to me and asked me to help the company by going to the bank and assisting them in raising some money. I felt, as a director of this company, that my honour was involved in having that road completed and in seeing that the wages of the men were paid. I felt that if we allowed that enterprise to collapse and break down before the road was completed to the coal fields it would be a public disaster and, to assist the company, I remember upon more than one occasion going to the bank, to Mr. Stavert, who was then manager of the bank and who now occupies a prominent position in the Bank of Montreal-and I make this statement publicly because I know that he will remember what I am now stating-and that, upon my persuasion and upon my consenting, with Mr. Barnes, to endorse the notes of the company, moneys were advanced for the purpose of enabling Mr. Barnes to go to Norton and away to the end of the track by special' train that afternoon for the purpose of paying these men. These are the only cases in which the proceeds of any notes came Into my possession.
These moneys were handed at once to the contractor and they were necessary to enable him to pay the labour bills and the other charges. I want to say for Mr. Al-

len. the secretary of the company, that wherever there was a note discounted where it was not done through himself, and there were comparatively few except in the way of renewals, he always made an accurate statement with regard to the notes and with regard to the proceeds of them, and in every case he appeared to be and I believe was seeing that the proceeds were used for the legitimate purposes of the company. Mr. Allen is dead, but I am satisfied that were he living he would corroborate the statement I make. I am satisfied he gave satisfactory evidence to Mr. Sharpe, the auditor, that the moneys which came into his hands or into the hands of any others for the company were properly applied. Mr. Sharpe was appointed to audit the books of the company in the early part of the year 1904, I think, and his appointment was by direction of the government. At that time the company was making application to the government for further assistance, and we were greatly in doubt as to what course to pursue. We recognized that the cost of the road had run greatly beyond what we anticipated, and that if the enterprise was to be carried to a conclusion assistance would have to be given. It has been intimated in this report of the commission, nay it has been more than intimated that we had some object in view in not keeping accounts and that we were willing that the treasury should be looted, and that the moneys of this company should be taken by any one who wanted to get hold of them. I want to ask you, Sir, if it is consistent with such a suggestion, that when this company wanted further assistance in the winter of 1904, we said to them: 'We shall give you no further assist ance until an auditor has been appointed and the books have been gone over from beginning to end, and all the expenses of the company gone into most carefully, and then and then only will we consider whether or not we shall give assistance.' Is that the conduct of men who intended to do wrong; is that the conduct of men who were careless of the public interest? Notwithstanding that the company was greatly embarrassed, the government refused to give further assistance to them until that audit was made. Mr. Sharpe, who made that audit was the one man in New Brunswick who seemed to be recognized by all as most competent to do work of that character. He was an able man, he had a large practice, he was a man of great experience and I believe he did his work thoroughly. He made up an account of the cost of the road and I believe the commissioners say that if you take off the interest and the salaries from Mr. Sharpe's Mr. PUGSLET.
report which were not included in Mr. Evan's statement, there was only a difference of $159 between his report and Mr.. Sharpe's report. Mr. Sharpe was handed over all the accounts, he was given authority to get a full statement from the banks in St. John, he got all the cheques and all the vouchers-vouchers from Mr. Trueman and others, and he was directed to go into the accounts most thoroughly so as to satisfy himself as to their correctness. And Sir, I want to say that although Mr Sharpe had been engaged for months in this work, yet up to the time in the latter part of June, or the early part of July, 1904, when I left for England on business, although I had many conversations with him, he never intimated to me that he had found any difficulty in auditing the accounts or that there was anything in connection with the expenditures which was not absolutely proper and right. I received a leitter a few days ago from a gentleman who is not a political friend of mine but who I believe was actuated by a sense of justice. I refer to Mr. J. J. F. Winslow, of Fredericton and he states that in his judgment the interest allowed by the commissioners is not very much over one half of what it ought to be. He was in Mr. Allen's office and with the late Mr. Sharpe, during a considerable part of the time he was engaged in the work of auditing the accounts, and Mr. Winslow says:
I might add that during all the time in which I was engaged by Mr. Sharpe upon this work he never for one moment intimated in any way to me that he considered any moneys were misappropriated.
It does seem to me that the testimony of such a man should have weight, particularly in view of the manner in which this report has evidently been prepared, and in view of the criticism I have made on many statements contained in it.
There is another statement which is false. These commissioners make the statement that there was $11,500 paid by the company in 1901, to Mr. Evans, for bridge plans and surveys and transfer of subsidies, and they say at page 6 in effect that this was included in the option from Messrs. Clarke & Company and Drexell & Company. I suppose that in this statement they seek to convey the impression that it was improvident to pay the $11,500 in addition to the money which was paid for the purchase of the Central. There is no foundation for that statement. There is nothing in the evidence to warrant that statement. These plans, these surveys, these rights were for the part beyond Chipman, and formed no part of the railway between Norton and Chipman,

and did not pass in any way under the option from Clarke & Company and Drex-ell & Company to Mr. Evans. Then these commissioners say, on page 30, that the $11,500 paid for these plans were the first money which the provincial government paid to the company in 1901. That statement is also not supported by evidence. The government did not pay that $11,500. All the subsidies which were payable by the government were paid either to Mr. Barnes under the order he had, or were paid to the People's Bank of New Brunswick, which had an assignment of the subsidies from the provincial government. I do not know why this statement is made, but at all events there is nothing whatever in the evidence to warrant the commissioners in making it.

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: Did the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company have any money except what they got from the government?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: This money was borrowed by the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company from the bank.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Not at all, my hon. friend is wrong about that. What these commissioners state is that this was the first money which was paid by the government in 1901. That money was not paid by the government but it was paid by the company. The . money was borrowed from the bank, it formed a part of the expenditure of the company, and it would afterwards be covered by the bonds of the company which were guaranteed by the province. But it was not paid by the province in the sense in which these commissioners put it. They would lead the public to believe that this money was one of the first payments made and that it was paid out of the subsidy.
In that connection, I want to correct an impression which the report is calculated to convey, that from the very outset the government was to guarantee the bonds for the purchase of the Central Railway. It was nothing of the kind. The government, in the exercise of its judgment, thought it best that the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company should amalgamate with or acquire the Central Railway Company; but they had no thought in 1901 nor in 1902, of guaranteeing the bonds for the purchase of the Central Railway. If my hon. friend will turn to the synoptic report of the de-181
bates of the New Brunswick Assembly for 1902, he will find that the premier, in answer to a question, then stated that the company had made a proposition under which they were going to buy the Central Railway by means of an issue of six per cent bonds which they were then about negotiating; and Mr. Tweedie as Provincial Secretary stated that the government were in considerable doubt as to the propriety of allowing that to be done, because he said that in case there was one set of bonds on the Central Railway, which was the connecting link between this new line and the Intercolonial, and another set of bonds on the new line from Minto extending westward, guaranteed by the government, in case of default, the railways might again become separated into two systems, and the new line would be at the mercy of the line extending from Chipman to Norton. It was only when the legislature met in 1903, that the government came to the conclusion that they would guarantee bonds sufficient to enable the company to complete its purchase of the Central Railway and complete the improvements then being made, and make an issue of new bonds on the entire system, so that in reality and for all time the entire line, which is sixty miles in length, and including branches of eight or nine miles, should form one system of railway. I speak of that because the conditions would be somewhat different in the first instance if the government had guaranteed the bonds for the purchase of the Central Railway. At the time the option was acquired from Messrs. Evans & Elkins there was no thought of that. The acquiring of that option was the business of the New Brunswick Coal & Railway Company alone. It was some two years afterwards that the government decided, in the then condition of affairs to guarantee bonds on the entire system and wipe out the old issue which was standing against the new line.
I want to come to another statement which I think is unfair and not supported by the evidence. You will find on page 43 a reference to myself. Perhaps I ought not to deal with this, but rather leave it to my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) if he should do us the favour of making some remarks, because the matter was I think brought particularly to his attention. But as it concerns myself, I think I perhaps ought again to call attention to the unfairness of these commissioners. It appeared in my evidence that the $5,000 which has been spoken of as having the initials 'W.P.' opposite it, was a cheque given on the 30th of June, 1904, just before I was leaving for England, to the order of the New Brunswick Real Estate Loan & Trust Company.



These commissioners refer to this company as a loan company, and make the statement that it kept no books. Well, Sir, a loftn company carrying on the business of a loan company which kept no books would be an extraordinary institution; yet they convey that impression. As a matter of fact, although the name of this company is the New Brunswick Real Estate Loan & Trust Company, it has never done any business as a loan company or a trust company. It is simply a real estate holding company, holding the Pugsley Building in the city of St. John; and what I said was that Judge Trueman, who was the Secretary and the Treasurer of this Company, kept ordinary rent books, in which rents, taxes, and the general disbursements of the building would be entered. I explained that it was a real estate holding company and that was all the business it was doing. But these commissioners put forward the suggestion that it was a loan company in order to discredit the evidence I gave, a proceeding which it strikes me was not fair and not what one might expect from commissioners claiming to be regarded as non-partisan. I also stated that the cheques of this -company were given by myself and my wife, because we were the owners of the stock in the company, and we had in the Bank of New Brunswick a considerable amount of money which belonged to this company having been received from the sale of western lands belonging to the company, but which had been put in our names in order to ear-mark it, as it were, so as to keep it apart from the ordinary real estate business of the company; and I produced before these commissioners the cheques dated on the dates given on page 43, except the last one, which should be March, 1904, instead of 1902, and I stated what the amounts were for as shown in the cheque stubs and in the cheques themselves: one in favour of E. C. Elkin for $2,000, another in favour of E. G. Evans for $2,000, another to A. I. Trueman, for $2 750 another in favour of A. I. Trueman for $198; another in favour of E. G. Evans for $1,000; and another in favour of the Canada Permanent Loan Company for $1,272, being for interest for the half year due on the 1st of March, 1904. I stated that positively. I stated that I remembered distinctly paying the interest to the Canada Permanent, and loaning this money to the railway company for that purpose, and I actually produced before the commissioners the receipt of the Canada Permanent Company for the payment. I also stated that in order to make a payment to Evans & Elkins on their option, the company had borrowed money from a number of people in St. John, whom I Mr. PUGSLEY.
named-Mr. Frank Stetson, Mr. McAvity, Mr. Connell, Mr. Barnhill, Mr. Trueman, and Mr. Skinner. I said that the company had paid one-half of the amount, and that there was a balance of $2,750 due, for which those people held notes, and that was the amount of the cheque which we lent through Judge Trueman to the railway company. I not only gave the names of these people, but produced the cheque in favour of Judge Trueman. I remember as if it were yesterday that after I produced the cheques Mr. Powell said: 'You need not mind going any further; you have the cheques,' I said, 'Yes, it is fortunate that I have the cheques.' Yet, notwithstanding that, these commisioners choose to distort the record and say that I was not sure that these moneys were loaned to the New Brunswick Coal & Railway Company, but surmised that they had been loaned. The record shows that I stated positively that I loaned these moneys and produced the cheques and the cheque stubs to verify the statement I made; yet they chose to to throw doubt upon my statement and say that if I did lend it no doubt I got the money back. All I can say is there is the testimony which I gave, and I produced the cheque stubs which contain the memos made at the time; and if they wanted to discredit my testimony, they ought to have called Mr. Connell and Mr. Barnhill who, they say, gave exceedingly satisfactory testimony, and these other gentlemen, and asked them if it were true this amount was lent the company and this $2,750 was paid under the circumstances and the notes given^ up to Mr. Trueman. Should they not h'ave done that before throwing aside the testimony I gave that the loan was for the purposes of the company and was a loan to the companies.
There is another matter with regard to which these commissioners have done a great wrong to those who were interested in the carrying forward of this undertaking and to Mr. Evans, a member of the firm of Evans & Elkin who gave the option to the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company upon the Central Road. * The statement which was made by Mr. Evans was-and the document was produced- that having an option on the bonds and two-thirds of the stock of the Central Road, he and Mr. Elkin gave an agreement to sell the road and give a complete title to the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company for the sum of $180,000. He also said that there was then important work under way, work of reconstruction of bridges and trestles and certain other improvements, on which some $24,000 had been already expended and which, it was estimated, would cost something like $50,000 more, and he swore that they went on and completed those improvements be-

fore the New Brunswick Coal and Kailway
Company took over the road. They completed those improvements at their own expense, outside the money altogether which the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company expended on that line. But these commissioners say:	Why, we cannot believe Mr. Evans, because he was not under a written obligation to make those improvements; true, he was under a moral obligation, but not under a written obligation, and it passes our comprehension that a man like Evans could be so honest as to carry out what he was only obliged to do by a verbal and moral obligation. Well, the answer to this statement is two-fold. First, that there is nothing in the conduct of Mr. Evans, from beginning to end, which would warrant these commissioners in refusing to believe him; and second, that this was an option which the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company held upon the Central; and if Evans and Elkin had not carried out in good faith what they had undertaken to do, the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company would not have been bound to exercise, and would not have exercised, their option, and Evans and Elkin would not have succeeded in selling the road. But Mr. Evans produced a ledger showing the payments from month to month; and if these commissioners had wanted the details, all they had to do was to send to Mr. Fowler at Norton, who was keeping account of the expenditure, and he would show it in detail. But they did not want that, they did not ask it, and they tried to throw discredit on the testimony of Mr. Evans in this way.
They say that they got no explanations about' that expenditure. Well, I was on the stand and they never asked me about RJ. The commissioners go out of their way, in another part of their report, to say that they looked upon me-and my hon friend from Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has said the same thing-as having the whole management of the road-that I was, to all intents and purposes, managing director Yet, when I was upon the stand they did not ask me to explain why Evans and Elkin spent $74,000 on the improvement of the Central. Had I been asked, I would have been able to state that, before making a payment on the Central, the representatives of the railway company, which held the option, examined from time to time the accounts and books of Evans and Elkin and saw the moneys they were expending on improvements. And Evans and Elkin submitted to me, as I stated in the legislature, their statement showing they had expended a total of $74,000 on improvements on the Central Railway. Yet, without asking me a single question with regard to it, without apparently making any effort to get 'hold of the books
181 i
kept by Mr. Fowler, which would show the details, and in the face of the positive testimony of Mr. Evans, the commissioners discarded his testimony because they could not believe that any man would be honest enough to carry out an obligation which was only a verbal and a moral, one. If that be the idea of the commissioners, as to the motives and impulses which would influence an ordinary, honest man, they are welcome to it. But there is the fact that these expenditures were made and that the accounts were duly shown the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company before that company exercised its option and completed the purchase of the road.
On page 59 the commissioners say:
The apparent object of the company, judging from results, was to secure the moneys provided by the Act without any effort to establish a plant, and the apparent functions of the executive, judged hy the same standard, was to make the way easy and profitable to the company to accomplish that object.
Let me say that although, in the first instance, the legislature provided that a mining plant should bo established, y@t in the progress of events, that policy was departed from, and it was determined that the better way to secure the development of the coal areas was to encourage the men who were already engaged in a small way in these mining operations, to build branch lines to the various lines so as to facilitate the output of coal and to place it on the market. That was explained to the legislature prior to the passing of the Act of 1904, and by that Act the company was relieved from the obligation of establishing a mining plant. They were relieved of this obli-gaton because the legislature chose to substitute the obligation to build branch lines in the place of the obligation to establishng a mining plant.	.	,,,
Again the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) says that these commissioners justly attack the members of the provincial government, and particularly myself, for the statements which were made, when _ assistance was being asked from the legislature for this company, with regard to the coal deposits and the ability to turn out 150,000 tons per annum and the possibility of finding a market for the output. Sir, I do not take back one word of, what I said regarding the possibility of developing ^the coal areas of New Brunsiwck. Let me call attention for a moment to the development which has already taken place, notwithstanding the fact that we have not been able to sell as much coal to the Intercolonial Railway as we were led to believe we would be able to do. Let me show the progress this road has been making as a result of its extension to the coal fields. When the road was undertaken in 1901, the total freight carried over it was 5,410

tons and the number of passengers, 946. Here is a statement of the different years:

And, Sir, I have no doubt, in a very few years, with the rising popularity of New Brunswick coal upon the market, with th increased number of men who are being induced to come there and settle down an live in cottages which the various coa owners are building, and in view of th fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific is com ing there, that the expectations which I held out to the legislature and people of New Brunswick will be far more than realized, and that it will not be many years before there will be considerably more than 150,000 tons of coal a year produced in these coal mines in the vicinity of Minto. And yet these commissioners make that a serious ground of attack upon us, say that we were deceiving the legislature, and that we ought to be condemned by the general public. And my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Crothers) says that for that reason among others we ought to be condemned by this parliament, and that action ought to be taken with reference specially to myself.
I wish to call attention to another instance of the unfairness of these commissioners. At page 33 they seek to convey the impression that there has been somei thing very lax. And here I would invite the attention of the hon. gentlemen who are seeking to figure out the interest:
As the bonds were dated July 1, 1903, it will be seen that three coupons on each bond, covering a year and a half, until December 31, 1904, being a year and a half interest on $450,000 bonds at 4 per cent (amounting to $27,000) had previously accrued. Apparently the most of these three coupons had never been cashed, and we could not find out what disposition was made of them. They should have been cut off by Mr. McAvity and cancelled, and a reoord kept of the same. There is no guarantee that at some time in the future some of these coupons may not be presented for payment by holders for value.
Well, Sir, four years have passed away and they have never been presented yet, and I think we may reasonably conclude that they never will be presented. As a matter of fact, I am informed, they were cut off and cancelled. These commissioners say they were not paid by the province. They were attended to by the company which had borrowed money upon them. They were cut off and cancelled, and though these commissioners say they 'could not find out what disposition was made of them,' they should have been cut off by Mr. McAvity and cancelled, Mr. PUGSLEY.
what will you say, Mr. Speaker, and what will this House say as to the fairness of the commissioners when I tell you that I am informed by telegram from Mr. McAvity that upon the stand he was never asked a single question with regard to these coupons?-his attention was never called to them. Yet these commissioners coolly put it forward as if there might be some dreadful harm come to the province if these coupons should turn up. Could not find out what had become of them! Why did not they ask those who knew? These commissioners seem to think that the way to find out these things is to ask the people who know nothing about them, and to refrain from asking those who do Know, and then throw out the suggestion that they have not been able to get the information. Again, they make the reflection, on page 33, because in the office of the Receiver General there was not a statement as to the amount of bonds which had been guaranteed. I am not sure but that that would have been the proper place to have that record; it may have been an oversight that it was not sent there. But in the office of the Executive Council to which Mr. Powell, the counsel, and the commissioners had access-because it is in evidence that Mr. Powell had gone over all the records of the Executive Council with regard to the company-there were the orders in council drafted from time to time for the guaranteeing of these bonds, and a statement of what had been guaranteed, giving the amounts and the date of guarantee. But these gentlemen say they have only got information on this point from Mr. Shadbolt, manager of the Royal Trust Company, of St. John, who had a clear record of the matter. I do not know whether misapprehension of Mr. Shad-bolt's duty led the commissioners into making some of the extraordinary statements they made as to the time when these bonds were guaranteed and the amounts, because they have evidently ignored the orders in council and have made absolutely false statements as to the amount guaranteed, in some cases going so far as to say they were guaranteed in advance of the legislative authoritv for that purpose. But Mr. Shadbolt, in the ordinary course of business, would not have the time when the bonds were guaranteed, what he would have would be the time when, as trustee, he countersigned the bonds, when the issue would be made. As a matter of fact, with regard to the $250,000, they were made as one issue, because they were to rank pari passu, and, if my memory serves me, were left with the People's Bank for safe keeping, to be issued from time to time as required. Mr. Shadbolt could show when they were counter-

signed, but not when the Provincial Secretary guaranteed them. I have a telegram from Mr. Shadbolt in which he says, confirming what I have said, that he knows when $338,500 was countersigned up to August 6, because that is the time when the exchange took place, and I think he knows when another small amount was guaranteed, but as to the others he knows nothing as to when they were guaranteed. Yet these commissioners have taken his evidence as to the time when they were guaranteed. But, as I have said, there were the orders in council showing the bonds guaranteed at different times. I repeat, and repeat as emphatically as possible, that the statements which these commissioners have made in various parts of their report, contradictory statements in some cases, are contrary to the evidence, and the commissioners have no warrant for making them.	,
Now, these commissioners say that, in figuring out this shortage, they have no doubt that this $39,000 which they say was the shortage on what they found paid to Messrs. Evans & Elkin form a part of the total shortage. How naive are these commissioners! They had to put that in to make the total shortage, and they made it for that purpose. These commissioners gravely say that they have no doubt it does form part of the total shortage, when nobody else would dream but that they had put it there for the very purpose of making the deficit as large as possible. Let me repeat just what I have casually mentioned, and that is that the statement that was made to the auditor, Mr. Sharpe, by Mr. Allen, the secretary of the company, that the amount .paid to the Central Railway was $180,000, that that, in my belief, was a correct statement, and that Mr. Sharpe was quite justified in making the statement in his audit.
Bear in mind that the agreement which was made in the first place was for $180,-
000.	No one questions that being a bona fide contract entered into between Messrs. Evans and Elkin and the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company. It is true that these commissioners say that if the company had held out for a while they might have been able to squeeze these people into allowing the to ad to go at a smaller figure. I dispute that. There had been a very considerable public agitation before this option was acquired for the development of the coal areas. The policy of the government and the legislature, approved of by both sides of the House, was to develop these coal areas. Messrs. Evans and Elkin had an option upon the bonds of this road and knowing that it formed the connecting link between the coal fields and the Intercolonial Railway, where
the best market for the coal would be obtained, and they would not be disposed to part lightly with this road, particularly when it was well ironed, when it was well known that the steel rails, spikes and bolts alone would be worth pretty nearly $4,000 a mile, the amount which it had been agreed to pay for this railway, and bearing in mind also that Evans and Elkin were to complete the improvements they then had under way, and which, as their accounts showed, amounted to somewhere in the vicinity of $74,000, it did not strike the government or myself, as ex officio member of this company, that the price of $4,000 a mile was an unreasonable price to pay for this road. It did not strike me that, knowing this was our policy, to develop the coal areas, anything would be gained by waiting and we thought it wa9 a reasonable proposition to pay $180,000, or $4,000 a mile for the 45 miles, upon their giving a complete and absolute title to the line and also making these improvements which they then had under way. That was the agreement, Messrs. Evans and Elkin were entitled to the $180,000 on their completing the title, but not until then. As the evidence shows, as the matter went along, it was found that there were other shareholders besides those whom Messrs. Evans and Elkin represented, whose holdings amounted to something like $300,000. Among them Dr. de Bertram was only one. Whether there were others interested with Dr. de Bertram in his stock or not, I do not-know, but there were other shareholders for whom Messrs. Trueman and Allen were acting and they represented to Mr. Evans that their clients, people interested in the minority stock of the company, were not satisfied that they should receive the whole amount of $180,000 and it was stated that Messrs. Evans and Elkin, while they wanted to get out of it as much of their contract price as they could, did not want to have a foreclosure suit which would mean a long delay and great expense. The evidence shows that they were informed that it was claimed by these shareholders that the bondholders were mortgagees in possession and various questions as to what they had earned or might have earned would necessarily arise _ in a suit for foreclosure. They were willing that the amount should be given by Messrs. Allen and Trueman to the other shareholders and I find that along in the winter of 1903, when Mr. Evans gave to the secretary of the company a receipt for $60,000, the four first payments of $15,000 each, he did allow Mr. Allen to use a -part of that money to satisfy the demands of the other shareholders. It went on down to the summer of 1903 when Mr. Evans and Mr. Allen consented to take something in the vicinity of $140,000, leaving it to Mr. Trueman and Mr. Allen to

do what was reasonably necessary to acquire the property and satisfy the minority shareholders in this company.

That was the duty of the commissioners and why did they not do it? These commissioners were charged with the duty of doing it. They	were charged with the duty of reporting as to the receipts and the expenditures of this oompany. Although Mr. Hazen, the premier, is a director ex officio of this company and was then, and although the provincial secretary was then and is now an ex officio member of this company they did not choose themselves to ascertain what had been the expenditures but they charged this commission with the duty of doing it and they gave them power of summoning before them all parties and having, brought before them all books, and all accounts. And the hon. member from Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has put this before the House as a report which is worthy of the confidence of this House and upon which the House should Act. And, when asked as to how this interest account was made up, the premier of New Brunswick said it would take months to make out a statement as to how they arrived at the interest. What I do submit to the members of this House and to the people of this country with all confidence is that when these commissioners issued this report they ought to have ensured that the interest amount was absolutely accurate; they ought to have known that it could be relied upon. Now, Sir, what do these commissioners recommend? They recommend that the directors of this company, and more especially the ex officio directors, the Hon. Mr. Tweedie and myself, should be called to render an account to this company for its receipts and expenditures. Sir, I have always been ready to render an account of my dealings with this company as an ex officio director. I would have been glad if, instead of transferring the matter to this forum and taking up the time of this parliament, the provincial government had taken some steps to carry out the recommendations of these commissioners and to have an account taken. But, Sir, the legislature of New Brunswick has now been prorogued and no action of any kind was taken on this report by the provincial government. The only reference that was , made to it so far as I have observed, and I read the papers daily, was to put two series of questions to the government, one of which was answered in the manner to which I have directed attention. Sir, I have waited until now, waited since the last of March, when this report was signed and published. I have waited until now for some action to be taken on the part of the provincial government to have the report of these commissioners carried out and to have some steps taken to have an accounting. They have not chosen to take any steps to that end, although under the law the present Attorney General and the present Provincial Secretary are ex officio directors of the company and are entitled

to call upon me and every other director for .an accounting. They have taken no steps to do so, and whv ? Because they knew that if they brought an action in the Supreme Court in Equity, the objection would probably be raised in this parliament that the matter was sub judice and therefore could not properly be brought up in this parliament, and they would have been further away than ever from their cherished design of driving me from the government. They have not done so, and I have taken the only course open to me: I yesterday instructed my solicitor-the legislature having prorogued only a few days ago, to issue a summons in the Supreme Court of Equity of the province of New Brunswick, making the New Brunswick Coal and Kailway Company and the other parties defendants, so as to bring all parties before the court for the purpose of having an accounting as to the receipts and expenditures made by that company, and for the purpose of having a decree made as to the state of its accounts. Having taken that course, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that I have done all that I can properly do, and what it is right and proper that I should do.
While I may not perhaps be as careful as I ought to be, particularly in reference to my own affairs, and although in respect to those loans which were made to the company, I ought perhaps to have taken a receipt or a promissory note from the company, yet I want to say that the man has yet to live who can stand up and say that I have ever wronged an individual or the public in respect to a single dollar. I have always been prepared, in the legisla ture of New Brunswick, where I spent many years, and before the people of the province, who know me, to meet any charges that have ever been made or can be made with regard to myself. In this parliament I am a comparative stranger, but I have endeavoured to present the facts of the case as I believe them to be. I have endeavoured to point out errors, inconsistencies, falsehoods, inaccuracies of the grossest kind, evidences of the greatest partisanship, in this report. I think I can acquit my conscience of having done anything but what I should do in presenting the facts of the case to this House.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit myself to the judgment of this House. I recognize that I could not remain a member of this House or a member of this government if I ceased to have the respect and regard of the members of this House. I feel that I could no longer be worthy to sit among hon. gentlemen who occupy seats in this House if I had been guilty of any act unworthy of a public man. I desire therefore to leave my case in the judgment of Mr. PUGSLEY.
this House; and, Sir, with your permission, in order that the members on both sides of the House may feel the more free to discuss this case and comment upon it, I will ask the liberty to retire while the discussion is going on and until the House comes to a conclusion upon it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not have thought that any hon. member of this House, much less one occupying the responsible position of a Minister of the Crown, would have ventured to defend himself against such grave findings as are contained in the report of this Royal Commission, upon such flimsy pretexts as those that have been advanced by the Minister of Public Works this afternoon and this evening. I ask hon. members on both sides of this House to ponder for a moment the passages which have been quoted from that report by my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers), and then ask themselves if in all the heat and verbosity and repetition which the Minister of Public Works has exhibited, there is one single statement that breaks dowm or in any way impairs the force of the arraignment with which he stands confronted before the country to-day. 1 ask the members of this House what they think of all this talk about a typographical error, which does not affect in the slightest degree one single transaction of the very many transactions for which this commission has condemned the Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend from West Elgin Iras already dealt with that typographical error. I was surprised that the Minister of Public Works would attempt in this House to represent that that error in the statement regarding the_ capital stock of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company was a deliberate attempt on the part of the commission to deceive the public. Why, if the hon. minister had looked at the opposite page of the report he would have seen that the commission set out fully that the capital stock of the company was $100,000 and that the number of shares Mr. Skinner disposed of amounted to $43,000, and could not possibly have amounted to $430,000. But, Mr. Speaker, as in a former case in which the Minister of Public Works was involved, this typographical error has been used for the purpose of drawing a herring across the trail. Now, Mr. Speaker,
I have read with the greatest care this report, I have Tead also with the greatest care the evidence on which that report is founded, and I am prepared to say, speaking as a member of this House, thatothere is not one accusation or finding in that report that is not absolutely borne out by the evidence. The Minister of Public Works has stated in his closing remarks that he has endeavoured to show the inconsistencies and errors and mistakes that

appeared in that report. I am here to-night to show by the evidence, which I have with me, that the statement which the hon. gentleman has made to this House to-night with reference to these matters is absolutely contradicted by the evidence, and much of it by his own statement before the commission; 'and I regret very much that the Minister of Public Works, under the pretext of giving us an opportunity of discussing this question freely should have seen fit to withdraw from this House, because I intended to put a few questions to him in reference to the matters which I say he has represented, in a false manner before this House.

And also as has been pointed out, not one of them put a single dollar into the treasury of the company; every dollar that the company handled they got out of the treasury of the province of New Brunswick or out of the treasury of the federal government at Ottawa.
Now, the Minister of Public Works has sought to cast discredit upon this commission by representing to this House that they were not justified in the statement that this company kept no books, and he- rather ingeniously, I thought-quoted from the report the statement in Teferertce to the books which were kept at Norton and which related to the portion of the Central road from Norton to Ohipman, and asked the members of the House, in view' of that statement, what they thought of the statement that this company had no books or records. Why, at the very bottom of the page from which the minister quoted was a statement that outside of these books there were no records kept by the company, and more than once in their report the commissioners state that the books at Norton and so far as that portion of the road was concerned were well kept. But the books, the lack of which the commissioners comment upon, are books relating to the construction of the so-called 15-mile section and the other expenditures in connection with the purchase of the Central Railway and the receipt and disposal of moneys^ procured as subsidies and raised upon bonds, &c. This company was incorporated in 1901 to build a line of railway from Chipman to Gibson, opposite the city of Fredericton, a distance of 45 miles. A contract was entered into between the government and the company, the government grants ing the subsidy for the building of that line. There is not a book to be found, and there was not. a book available for the examination of this commission with reference to that portion of the work. There was a secretary to that company, and a treasurer and a president. The Minister of Public Works referred to J. J. F. Winslow, of Fredericton, who became, after the death of Mr. G. W. Allen, the secretary of the company, and who, in Mr. Allen's lifetime, acted as his clerk. And it appears by the evidence of Mr. Winslow, who was actually the secretary of this company, that he did not know even who the treasurer of the company was, that Mr. Allen kept no books, that he (Mr. Winslow) after he became secretary, endeavoured to make up a book from scattered data which Mr. Allen furnished him, a statement which is on the face of it incoml-plete, and which never professed-and nobody ever stated that it professed-to represent the complete transactions of the company. It is in the evidence of Mr. McAvity that he had no books. He states

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND EE-POKT OF THE CENTEAL BAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
in his evidence not only that he had no books, but that he could not find any books except the books of the company at Norton. And there had been no contention made, until the effort of the Minister of Public Works to-day, to controvert the statement that there were no records or books of account that could be relied upon to show the expenditure of the large amount of money that passed through the hands of the company. Not only had this company no books of account, but the books of account of the Barnes Construction Company to whom they let the contract for the construction of the Fredericton-Gibson section were not available. The Minister of Public Works sought this evening to create the impression that again this commission had attempted to deceive the public by stating that the company had no books by making reference to the statement that Mr. Shannon, the auditor of the Intercolonial Railway, made when he examined the books of the Barnes Company that he was making up a statement of cost for the purpose of obtaining a federal subsidy. Why, that statement appeared in the report itself, that Mr. Shannon had access to the books' that the Barnes Company had at the time. But when the commission sought to obtain these books, they were not available, the books had disappeared and the commission made an effort to find the books of the Barnes Construction Company, and notwithstanding this they were not produced before the commission. But I propose to read from the evidence of Mr. Barnes with reference to that. I refer to page 643 of the evidence:
Q. Have you any cheques or drafts that were given by you or accepted by you in connection with this transaction A. I did not keep track of them.
Q. Have you any cheques or drafts in connection with this matter between you and company?
A. I don't think it. The business was wiped out and that was the end of it.
Q. Did you destroy your drafts?
A. I did as a general thing. iQ. Your cheques?
A. I destroyed them. At the end of the year the cheques are checked over and that is the end of them.
Q. Is that your invariable custom ?
A. As a general thing I do.
Q. Have you heard any one tell of your books since?
A. No.
Q. Have no idea w'here they are?
A. No.
This is the evidence of the manager of the Barnes Construction Company with reference to the books which this commission sought to get before it, to determine as to the correctness of the payments made to him. Not only with reference to the Barnes Construction Company were books found to be missing, hut when we come to

the loans alleged to have been made by the New Brunswick Beal Estate, Loan, Trust and Investment Company, of which the minister was practically the sole owner, the evidence is that there were no books. I desire to give the evidence with reference to that, which will be found at page 697. Judge Trueman, of whom the Minister of Public Works made mention, was the secretary, it appeared, of this company, a company that kept no books and made loans without any record, and without charging interest:
C* I should like to know about the credits or payments made to you before this $5,000 was got by you?
A. If Judge Trueman were living, I would assume you could get it from him or from Mr. Allen, the secretary.
This, it will be understood, is the examination of the Minister of Public Works.
Q. Mr. Allen had no books?-A. Mr. Allen told me he was keeping a correct account.
Q. You cannot give us the amounts that were paid to you on account of these advances you made to Mr. Evans or the company or for the use of the company, down to the 1st day of July, 1904?-A. No, I can't; my reason is this, I keep no personal trace of my money matters at all.
This is the evidence of the Minister of Public Works:
Judge Trueman had a power of attorney and my secretary had power of attorney as well; these accounts I know were loaned and Judge Trueman reported to me on the 30tli of June that there was considerably more than $5,000 due to the company.
That is the New Brunswick Real Estate Loan and Investment Company.
Q. I was asking you if you could give us the amounts?-A. That is the reason.
Q. We are to understand that you did not keep books of your own financial transactions?-A. Yes, I could say that, I can say that I did not. Since I have Been in business I have kept partial books of accounts, no credit amounts. All these matters I trusted entirely to Mr. Allen and to Mr. Trueman.
Further, on page 698:
Judge Trueman was treasurer and secretary and was running the transactions.
And yet there is the statement of the Minister of Public Works that the secretary and treasurer of that company, with this name, the New Brunswick Beal Estate, Loan and Investment Company, carried on its business without keeping -any books. Yet the minister reflects upon the commission because they -had not brought before them the executor of the Trueman estate to question him with regard to Judge Trueman's books and papers. He does this although when before the commission he himself stated that there were no books kept by
this company. Not only in reference to these two companies-the Barnes Construction Company, to which thousands of dollars were ostensibly paid out of the treasury of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, and the New Brunswick Real Estate, Loan and Investment Company by which loans were 'alleged to be made to the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, were the books missing and the records lost, but even in regard to the firm of J. M. Robinson & Company, who discounted bonds to the amount of $373,000. Would you believe that when Mr. Robinson was before that commission and was -asked about the record of that transaction, he stated that he could not find his books or the record of that transaction.

There is a very interesting story in connection with how that difference of $22,500 was disposed of. I have already referred to the order in council of the 2nd of July, 1901, and that order in council, after providing for the payment oi a subsidy of $2,500 per mile to the company although the Act provided for $3,000 per mile, makes this further provision:
The Provincial Secretary also reports that there has been paid by the Receiver General to the Central Railway upon and on account of the subsidy of $3,000 per mile, payable under the said Act, 15 Vic., chap 34, in respect to the line between Chipman and Fredericton the sum of $13,000, and the said Central Railway Company has also lodged with the Receiver General orders against such subsidy to the additional amount of $8,500, and as the subsidy payable under such Act is $3,000 per mile, and the work done on said line has by reason of thfe lapse of time since it was done and for other reasons become of comparatively little value, he recommends that the said sum of $13,000 shall not be deducted from said subsidy, and also that the amount of such orders or such portion thereof as the Lieutenant Governor in Council may deem just, shall with the approval of the legislature be paid to the holder or holders of such orders, said amount to be paid pro rata as each section of 10 miles is completed.
